title: FlowSat
text:
The problem and the idea
A satellite image comes with information about where, when and how it was acquired. FlowSat combines text with geographic location, acquisition date, ground sampling distance and cloud cover to guide satellite image synthesis.
The model builds on a pretrained SANA flow-matching Diffusion Transformer. Its metadata encoder respects the geometry of each field: locations lie on a sphere, dates are cyclic, and sensor values vary across scales. A zero-initialised conditioning branch preserves the pretrained backbone at the start of fine-tuning.



Generated FlowSat samples from the paper’s Figure 1. These are model outputs, not satellite observations.

title: FlowSat
text:
Reported results
On fMoW-RGB, the paper reports FID 31.10 and CLIP score 0.3016 with 20 Euler sampling steps at the 125K checkpoint. The compared DiffusionSat model uses 100 steps. These are sampling-step counts, not a measured end-to-end speedup.
The paper’s Table 2 distinguishes a controlled DiffusionSat comparison from other published baselines, whose training data and evaluation details are not matched. The headline numbers apply to fMoW-RGB; they do not establish best performance on every dataset or metric.

title: FlowSat
text:
Build on it
For Earth-observation researchers, FlowSat offers an open starting point for text- and metadata-conditioned synthesis. The repository and project page provide the implementation and examples for further experiments.

“Metadata is what separates a satellite tile from a natural image”
— FlowSat, Section 3.5

The results establish image-generation performance on the evaluated benchmarks. Metadata-conditioned changes should not be interpreted as physically calibrated simulations.
Full title: FlowSat: Flow-Matching Diffusion Transformers with Metadata Conditioning for Satellite Image Generation.

text:
ES 654: My Foray into Machine Learning
My journey into Machine Learning began with securing an internship at BEES Lab, IISc Bangalore, after my sophomore year. This experience plunged me into the thrilling world of Machine Learning. As a newcomer, I found the field daunting, filled with advanced concepts and rapidly evolving technologies. It was challenging to grasp the essence of Machine Learning and delve deeper. I pondered on differentiating myself from being just another coder proficient in CNN architectures using PyTorch to understanding fundamental concepts like the impact of a single LayerNorm block on model performance, the role of regularization in inducing generality, and the importance of visualizing the workings of the so-called “black box” of a neural network. The learning curve seemed colossal. Fortuitously, it was during this time that I was introduced to the course ES 654, an introduction to Machine Learning, taught by Prof. Nipun.
From the very first class, where Prof. Nipun introduced us to the broad scope of AI, I knew this course would be a turning point in my career. His teaching approach made me realize the importance of understanding classical Machine Learning’s intuition, often overshadowed by implicit modeling in Neural Modelling Strategies. The course took us from implementing Decision Trees and various classical Machine Learning algorithms in pure Python to building neural networks from scratch. It illuminated the intuition behind optimization strategies and autograd workings. The structured learning helped solidify my foundation in Machine Learning. Particularly impactful were the on-paper tests, where we derived vectorized solutions to various problems, significantly boosting my confidence and understanding.

Embarking on a Journey with Sustainability Lab (SL)
Prof. Nipun’s course made my decision to join Sustainability lab abundantly clear to begin a journey of delving into research under his guidance. The best thing about Prof. Nipun was the way he streamlined the learning experience and crafted it individually for every single student. My initial task involved bug fixes in Pyro, a deep probabilistic programming library on Pytorch. This was my first foray into open-source ML contributions, and Prof. Nipun’s guidance was invaluable. I remember him hand-holding me in this task and giving me code suggestions before I made the commits. The best part was him celebrating with me on the small victory of the first PR getting merged! This marked the beginning of my deep dive into Bayesian Machine Learning, focusing on Gaussian Processes and Neural Kernel Networks, which became my primary areas of interest at SL.

Parallelly, I attended Prof. Nipun’s advanced course on Probabilistic Machine Learning, which complimented my research perfectly, enhancing my understanding of Gaussian Processes. The highlight of my time at SL were the weekly meetings with Prof. Nipun. His guidance extended beyond theoretical solutions to the nitty-gritty of implementation. His mentorship played a crucial role in my development, not just academically but also in how I approach problems in my current corporate research role at Skan. Our collaborative work, including contributions from fellow students Aadesh Desai and Zeel B Patel, was recognized at the NeurIPS workshop on Gaussian Processes in 2023.

He has a unique way of fostering a familial atmosphere in the lab, from celebrating Teacher’s Day to enjoying lab dinners and shared moments of humor. One of my most cherished memories is receiving a personalized message and a copy of “The One Thing” by Gary Keller and Jay Papasan from him. His ongoing support for students and alumni, including career guidance, reflects his dedication to nurturing a community of budding researchers.
My experiences at Sustainability Lab have been instrumental in shaping my journey as a researcher in Representation Learning and in my professional endeavors. The opportunity to work with Prof. Nipun and his unwavering support and teachings have left an indelible impact on my life and career and I am forever grateful for his support and mentorship.

title: Shillong to Cambridge via Sustainability Lab
text:
About me
I am Rishiraj Adhikary, the Sustainability Lab’s first PhD graduate. I am now a Postdoctoral Research Associate at the University of Cambridge. This is the story of how I got here — and how much of it I owe to the lab and its people.
My dream was to study at an IIT, renowned for its top-notch technical education. Like countless others, I did not secure admission during my undergraduate studies. So I went from Shillong to Guwahati and earned a BTech in Electronics Engineering from Gauhati University, after which I joined an IT firm. Then, one afternoon in the office, one thing led to another and I felt I should give an IIT another shot — this time for an MTech. My mother encouraged me to attempt postgraduate study at an IIT, so I moved back to Shillong to prepare for GATE. I worked diligently and qualified the exam, but my score still fell short of the marks required for IIT admission. Despite this, I firmly believe that hard work pays off.
During a brief stint at IIIT Sricity, I met Dr. Venkatesh Vinayakarao (a former colleague of Prof. Nipun at IIIT Delhi), who encouraged me to join an IIT as a research assistant so I could experience high-quality research firsthand. Eager to do so, I sent cold emails to several professors across the IITs. On February 4, 2019, after an online interview, I received an offer from Prof. Nipun Batra to work in his lab for three months.


The first day and beyond
On my first day, Prof. Nipun asked one of his undergraduate students, Deepak, to give me a tour of the campus. Along the way I met other UG students like Soham, and PG students Karan and Souvik. The atmosphere they created was warm and jovial, and as an introvert I felt genuinely welcome. Little did I know how much I would end up learning from these UG and PG colleagues. During group meetings, Deepak’s careful feedback sharpened how I understood a concept, and Soham was remarkable at almost everything — from hardware to web design to implementing machine-learning algorithms from scratch.


The first three months (March – June 2019)
My BTech in Electronics gave me solid experience with microcontrollers and sensors, so Prof. Nipun asked me to build a sensing system for the Water Treatment Plant at IIT Gandhinagar. Beyond the technical work, this let me meet the wonderful people who keep the campus running — like Vishnu Deth and Jyotish Kumar — who patiently explained how such a large campus receives, filters, and distributes its water. It was my first experience collaborating with the people who look after a critical campus asset.
After just two months, Prof. Nipun brought me into writing a research paper. He shared a draft in Google Docs full of pointers and asked me to fill in each section — explaining the experiments and data collection, and supporting every claim with a graph. That exercise taught me to make presentable figures, run efficient experiments, and document every task properly. Much of what I learned in this phase became the foundation of my PhD.



My first internship, in the winter of 2019, was at CEEW. Here I am working with geospatial data to study how aerosol optical depth changes over the Uttar Pradesh region of India.


The weekly group meetings were an integral part of lab life. I met wonderful students — Deepak, Apoorv, Soham, Rithwik, Karan, Souvik — and learned something from each of them.



A special-interest-group meeting on air pollution at AIIMS, New Delhi, in December 2019. (Good luck finding me!)


Near the end of those two months, Prof. Nipun asked whether I would be interested in pursuing a PhD. I was elated — I really wanted to spend more time at IIT Gandhinagar. My biggest fear was the PhD interview, and when I shared it, he reassured me: “Don’t worry — even if you don’t clear the interview, I will extend your JRF tenure and you can continue here.” That one sentence gave me the confidence to face it, and he went further, taking a mock interview to prepare me for the real one. Getting into the PhD program was one of the happiest days of my life.


The first year of the PhD (July 2019 – July 2020)
My excitement soon met the weight of coursework. Prof. Nipun reminded me that coursework is an integral part of learning and helps keep the mind engaged beyond research — which turned out to be true. Along the way I met many new people, and my circle on campus grew.
Then, after a semester and a couple of months on campus, COVID struck. Like many others, we moved back home amid the uncertainty. Prof. Nipun set up steady timelines, and at one point we met daily over Zoom to share progress. Meeting every day felt like a lot back then, but it was precisely those regular check-ins that got me my first publication. In the early PhD years we don’t yet appreciate how much effort a paper takes; during this time I had the chance to work with Prerna, Tanmay, and — for the first time — my own labmate, Zeel. All of them are in wonderful places today, and I am so glad to have this global network of friends.



During the early years, Prof. Nipun and I set up our very first lab bench in the workspace itself — acquiring the oscilloscope, power supply, and function generator took a lot of paperwork, but it was worth it. (September 2020)




The second year: rejections, and a turning point
Back on campus between periodic lockdowns, I was working steadily on a second project, SpiroMask. It took about 2.5 years for that work to finally be published, and every rejection stung — I had poured so much into it, including collecting breathing data while COVID was still a real concern.
I still remember the third rejection of the SpiroMask paper; it was the moment I felt closest to giving up. Rather than dwell on the setback, Prof. Nipun turned it into action — he began looking up fellowships I could apply to, hoping some good news might lift the mood. He found that the Fulbright fellowship application was still open, with about a week left to submit. I told him I shouldn’t bother, since it was so competitive I would never get it. His reply has stayed with me: “Do not self-reject — let them reject you first. Self-doubt shouldn’t stop us from applying.”
I eventually found the courage to apply. There was another hurdle: the application needed a letter of invitation from a US institution. I drafted one myself, Prof. Nipun emailed it to two labs in the US, and within 24 hours both replied with invitations. I remember standing in the Firpeal hostel lift when I saw his email carrying the invitation — that was all I needed to feel motivated again. It was proof that the work wasn’t in vain, and that some things simply need a little holding on. By October 2021, I was one of 30 recipients of the fellowship, and a few days later I also received the PMRF fellowship. Things were turning around, and the motivation to work harder came right back.



My birthday in 2020 — the whole CS group came out to celebrate, and I was overjoyed. Everyone in this photo is now in a wonderful place, from Assistant Professors at IITs and abroad to Research Scientists in top labs.




The third year: balancing teaching and research
Being a teaching assistant is an important part of a PhD, and most of the time it is genuinely rewarding. During one busy stretch in 2022, though, my teaching responsibilities began to overlap with a major paper deadline, and I was struggling to balance both. When Prof. Nipun noticed, he stepped in and helped rearrange my assignment so I could focus on the submission. It is exactly the kind of support that goes beyond research — making sure a student’s wellbeing and work don’t suffer — and it made a timely submission possible.


Five years is not only about research
When I returned to campus after my Fulbright tenure, I grew a little complacent and drifted for almost a month. Prof. Nipun nudged me to get back to work and resume meetings with my CMU advisor, Prof. Mayank Goel. A PhD is a grind, and five years is very little time to learn to do research, present, write, collect data, network, attend conferences, intern, and — most importantly — publish in good venues. These were hard skills to build, especially with no research training in my undergraduate years, and training me took a tremendous, often invisible amount of effort from Prof. Nipun. As he likes to say, hard work isn’t about arriving at the lab at 5 AM and leaving at 11 PM — it’s about giving even two solid, focused hours to research.


So close, yet so far
By the end of my PhD, I realized I had achieved far more than I ever dreamed of. On my first day I had simply prayed to spend as much time as possible at the institute and earn a doctorate. I got much more in return: multiple fellowships, a great network, and a mentor I think of as an elder brother. I sometimes joke to friends that, given my introverted and sensitive nature, I might not have completed a PhD with anyone else — this lab changed me for the better.
That lesson came with its challenges. In my last semester I found it hard to land a job; while others told me I had a strong profile, I couldn’t quite carry that into interviews. Prof. Nipun connected me with people in his network, and it eventually worked out — I joined JioThings as a Research Scientist. This was also when AI and LLM research were reshaping most labs. I had long held the view that I would only use AI to advance my real interest in ubiquitous health sensing, never work on it. That was naive, and it took me over a year to accept a simple truth: sometimes research directions need to pivot. The LLM experience I gained at Reliance later proved instrumental in my postdoc applications.


Research goes on
The Sustainability Lab changed my life. I came to earn a PhD from an IIT — that was my dream — and I left with far more than I had hoped for. Beyond the fellowships and the papers, I became a better person: more empathetic, more practical. I have recently joined the University of Cambridge as a Postdoctoral Research Associate, carrying every one of these lessons with me, and I hope to live up to what Prof. Nipun taught me.

title: The Growth Mindset: My Journey at the Sustainability Lab
text:
About Me
I worked for around two years at the Sustainability lab. My first work was in the summer of 2021, where I worked on Neural network approaches for non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM). This work was accepted at ACM Buildsys 2021, and I presented virtually at the conference. During my final year, I worked on quantifying uncertainty in NILM, collaborating and mentoring summer interns (Vibhuti, Rohit, and Haikoo). This work was accepted at ACM Buildsys 2022, and I presented it at Boston. Besides this, I was a TA for the Machine Learning course (ES654) taught by Prof. Nipun Batra. I have taken two courses, Operating System and Machine Learning, with Prof. Nipun Batra. Having collaborated with Prof. Nipun Batra for almost three years, Sustainability Lab feels like a second home. So I have summed up a few learnings from my time at the lab which are even helping me during my graduate studies.

title: The Growth Mindset: My Journey at the Sustainability Lab
section: Try to find opportunities inside your terrain first before searching outside.
text:
Try to find opportunities inside your terrain first before searching outside.
I used to believe that to get a good admission from a reputed university in the US, it is necessary to do a foreign research internship. I got a low rank in the entire electrical batch, which made it impossible for me to get a research internship through college. Still, I was so firm that I used to mail professors and Ph.D. students in the US and try to find some opportunity. Through this process, I got one reply from a Ph.D. student at CMU explaining to me that I should focus on doing good work rather than finding an internship at a good place. After reading this, I joined the Sustainability lab for my summer internship with Prof. Nipun Batra. I first encountered Prof. Nipun Batra during an Operating System course in the fall of 2021. After this, I took a machine learning course in the spring of 2021. His teaching style is very intuitive, which sparked my interest in machine learning. My summer internship work got me a paper at an international conference, and due to this, I received my Ph.D. admission at UMass Amherst. Through this experience, I learned that rather than running behind the tags, if you work hard at what you like, it pays off well.

title: The Growth Mindset: My Journey at the Sustainability Lab
section: You get ample opportunities if you want to work.
text:
You get ample opportunities if you want to work.
My entire summer 2021 internship was online. This was the first time an online internship was organized, and initially, we faced a lot of difficulties, but things got better with the process as we kept on discussing ideas. During my internship, I was never treated as a junior. Even as an Electrical Engineering student, Prof. Nipun Batra consistently showed confidence in me, assigning me an independent project. My ideas were valued equally, and I was treated on par with Ph.D. students. He involved me in industry meetings, providing insights beyond academia. In my last year, Prof. Batra gave me the opportunity to be a Teaching Assistant and my first academic talk for the Machine Learning course. This experience significantly boosted my confidence. I even got an opportunity to guide interns in Summer 2022. With a collective effort, we submitted a full paper at Buildsys 2022, marking a successful collaboration. Most of my academic “first times”, like my first paper, first talk, and first research talk, have happened at the lab only because Nipun Sir has always shown great confidence in me, which motivated me to work. You will always get an opportunity at the Sustainability lab if you try to put some effort into learning.

title: The Growth Mindset: My Journey at the Sustainability Lab
section: Small things will impact a lot in the long term.
text:
Small things will impact a lot in the long term.
During the paper submission process, it is pretty easy and fast to improve the writing without actually pointing out the mistakes in the student’s writing, but at the lab, I always got advice on what to improve and how it needed to be done. During my presentation at international conferences, Prof Nipun Batra helped me create and improve my presentation skills. I presented and recorded my presentation plenty of times, and he has patiently tried to improve my minute mistakes. We ultimately got positive reviews at the conference. During this experience, I learned that it would first seem a lot to do, but if you go with the flow, even small things impact on a large scale.

title: The Growth Mindset: My Journey at the Sustainability Lab
text:
Collaborative learning always helps.
During my internship and project courses, we had lab meetings. Lab meetings used to be great, where people working on different projects learn about each other’s work. Through this process, even without actually working on the projects, you will tend to get insights and challenges about the project, which can be helpful to you in the future. During the lab meetings, everyone was involved and tried to provide ideas or feedback for someone else’s work. Knowing so many projects and getting a broad picture of the ongoing research areas was great.

title: The Growth Mindset: My Journey at the Sustainability Lab
section: Rather than results, try to create meaningful relations.
text:
Rather than results, try to create meaningful relations.
My paper and admissions were small wins compared to what I have gained from my entire journey at the Sustainability Lab. By working with Prof. Nipun Batra for almost three years, rather than being a professional mentor, he has been my constant guide in all terms, from my health to my Ph.D. failures. Nipun Sir never fails to message me during my hard times in the US. I am grateful to have him as my lifelong mentor. Besides Prof. Nipun Batra, I have been fortunate enough to work and learn from some fantastic people in the lab: Zeel, Rishiraj, Dhruvi, Palak, Harsh, Shivam, Chris, Vibhuti, Haikoo, Rohit, Aadesh and Karm. I can always rely on them for guidance and support.

title: From Chemical Engineer to AI Researcher - My Pathway Through Sustainability Lab
text:
Abstract
I am Aditi Agarwal, I have graduated IIT Gandhinagar as a Chemical Engineer with a Minors in Computer Science. I am currently working with Google DeepMind as a PreDoctoral Researcher. This page summarizes the 3 semesters I have worked with Sustainability Lab and how the experiences have completely changed my career trajectory and views about research!
Keywords: Sustainability Lab, 11/10 Recommended, Real Flavour of Research, Best Mentor

Introduction
It would be an understatement to say that Sustainability Lab has completely changed the trajectory of my career. I had dreamt of being a Software Engineer from the age of 8. Computers were and are my Roman Empire, and younger me was always enticed by the idea of doing a job where I had to spend my entire day on a computer. How fascinating!
Coming to IIT Gandhinagar as a Chemical Engineering student, I always knew I would have to step the extra mile to achieve my goals. However, my journey was sweetened and streamlined by joining the Sustainability Lab and working under the guidance of Prof. Nipun Batra!


Neural Network Newbie
I joined the Sustainability Lab in my 6th semester. I remember the first time I visited Prof. Batra’s office, he asked me what I was interested in working on, and I naively mentioned that I wanted to build my own Neural Networks rather than using pre-trained models. Mind you, I had worked with two startups until then as a CV intern and an ML intern, but while I was able to ship code to production using fast.ai, play around with data, etc., I never had a core understanding of what Machine Learning really is. This is where the Sustainability Lab helped me.


A class I did not sleep in
I was also taking the coveted ES 654 course with Professor Batra at the time. I remember the first class of the course. Probably the only class in the entire duration of my BTech where I had a smile on my face throughout. Prof. Batra was showing us some videos on what AI is. I remember seeing a video of Amazon Go and being so fascinated and excited to finally learn a course because I wanted to and not because it was a graduation requirement. Simultaneously working with Sir in the lab, I remember, in the initial days, I took 3 weeks to correctly train a heteroskedastic MLP in Pytorch on a basic dataset. The catch was only to change the loss function, but my lack of understanding of core ML concepts led to me making numerous mistakes each time. What I really enjoyed during these three weeks was the fact that every time in the weekly meeting, Nipun Sir explained the loss function until I finally got it right. Then, I was extremely impatient, waiting every week to be given a “meatier” exercise rather than training a simple MLP. It is now that I realize how important this activity was for me. The latter half of the semester was smoother, and I was given a chance to play around with real-world data as well. That semester marked my first experience as a researcher as I also presented a poster at the UGRS.


Brick by Brick
In my seventh semester, in the last few days of summer, Prof. Batra offered me the brick kilns project. This was the project that quite literally changed my career trajectory and defined my interests. The project aimed to use satellite data for the detection of brick kilns across India. The novelty lay in using techniques to minimize the data and maximize the metrics of the model. We were working on a rather challenging deadline of submitting a paper to a sub-track in AAAI’23 in a matter of 20 days. Every day, we had meetings in the office with Sir and we would spend hours in the AI lab, getting the code to work and receiving outcomes. This was my first experience writing a manuscript and also learning how to present one’s work. Mind you, I have always been into writing and reading fiction. I thought of academic writing as “boring and flavorless.” It was when the process of writing the manuscript started that I realized how important building a story is in a research paper. On 16 August 2023, at 1705 hours, we ended up submitting the manuscript. It did not matter that it was rejected. But those 20 days gave me the real flavor of research.
Working on a project that directly impacts numerous people, their livelihoods, and the climate fueled my intent to pursue a career in research. We continued working on the project throughout the semester. In my final semester, in a spur of the moment, I decided to take up extra credits and work on a project to develop a screening system for mental health issues in students. This was a project done in collaboration with another lab in the institute. Again, this turned out to be an interesting experience because we experimented with multiple techniques in the beginning and ended up pivoting our approach to make our results more explainable and ethical.


The Prof. Batra Effect
What distinguishes the Sustainability Lab is Nipun Sir’s commitment to helping each and every student reach their full potential. As a Chemical Engineering student working in Computer Science and specifically in AI, I have more often than not had the feeling of not being good enough. Working with Prof. Batra has instilled a confidence in me that what matters is my work and not my branch. I owe my current position as a Pre-Doctoral Researcher at Google DeepMind to Prof. Batra for his invaluable guidance throughout. I remember running to him for interview help, preparation tips, how to write an SOP, tips on my personal website, and the LORs and personal notes. It was him who told me about the program at first and motivated me to apply for the same, not letting my doubts get the better of me. He always mentions, “Don’t self-reject.”
I have always been an individual who focuses on getting results. My definition of results meant something positive and quantitative, a 5% boost in accuracy, or a reduction in loss. Anything less would annoy me and make me feel as if whatever I did in the week was futile. Mind you, Prof. Batra too is an individual who focuses on the results. But the primary difference here is his ideology about the result. For him, results mean the insights and conclusions that one draws from any task or activity. I have seen the transition in the way I now present my work. It is always introduced by the motivation and the “why.” Sometimes I don’t even have results, but I am more often than not content with what I am presenting. This ideological change was again part of the Sustainability Lab experience.


Lab Legends
Prof. Batra bid us all farewell with a book and a personalized note. Coincidentally, it is also my favorite book, “Deep Work” by Cal Newport (a book I have annotated heavily and try to apply at least 10% of it in my life). Nipun Sir’s sense of humor and jovial energy always made me look forward to the weekly meetings. I remember, when his office was moved to the new Academic Block, he sent us a video guide as to how one can reach his office. Another fond memory I have is him sending me the contact details of a doctor in Gandhinagar because he got to know that I had injured my hand playing squash. I have countless such anecdotes that show his genuine care and concern towards his students. My journey at SL would be incomplete without mentioning all the amazing colleagues who became friends: Suraj Jaiswal, Madhav Kanda, Dhruv Patel, Rishabh Mondal, Zeel B Patel, Aadesh Desai, Eshan Gujarathi, Saagar Parikh. The lab dinner at Akshardham (I will not spoil the reason as to why we go to Akshardham). Little celebrations we have at the lab and fun conversations that take place before every meeting have left a positive imprint on me.
Consider this little article as my LOR to the Sustainability Lab to whomever it may concern 😊
This lab holds a very integral part of my BTech, and if you are an IITGn student who’s thinking about doing an internship/project with somebody, I would 11/10 recommend you to work at the Sustainability Lab.

title: Sustainability Lab: The Taste of True Research
section: A Cherry on the Top - SRE Award
text:
A Cherry on the Top - SRE Award
Research in itself became a rewarding experience with this incredible group, but receiving formal recognition made it even more special. The collective effort put into the project was truly worthwhile. title: Learning to Start from the Basics: My Journey at Sustainability Lab
text:
Starting from the Basics
Before joining the lab, I had already worked on a couple of projects in different research labs, so initially my approach was to directly think about how I could improve something. I started with the idea of improving the interpretability of Vision Language Models (VLMs) on thermal imagery.
But Nipun sir pushed me to first understand what was actually happening. Instead of immediately thinking about a solution, we started by analysing where the VLM was looking in the thermal image when given a particular query.
This analysis gave us some really interesting insights and eventually led me to think of a solution that was quite different from what I had initially imagined. This made me realise how important it is to understand a problem properly before trying to solve it.
Today, most things are built on top of increasingly complex architectures, and it is very easy to jump directly to a complicated solution. But sometimes, going back to the basics and asking “why?” can lead to much better ideas.


The Importance of Being Punctual
I also learnt how important it is to be punctual with a project. Research moves very fast today, and it is important to keep making progress and finish things on time. There is always a chance that someone else might independently think of a similar idea.
When I first joined the lab, I used to sulk at the idea of having weekly meetings. But I slowly realised how important they are in keeping the project moving.
When there is a big gap between deadlines, we tend to forget what we did, what we tried, and even what we were thinking at that point. Weekly meetings helped keep the flow of the project and made sure we always had something to work towards.


The Importance of Documentation
One thing I have tried to carry forward from the lab is the way Nipun sir organised everything.
Every part of the project was well documented, whether it was an experiment, a Streamlit demo, a result, or a presentation. These things can feel small while you are working on the project, but they help a lot later when you are writing a paper or preparing the final presentation.
Having everything documented also makes it much easier to go back and understand why certain decisions were made.


Lessons for Research
Overall, the Sustainability Lab changed the way I approach research.
I learnt that research is not always about immediately finding a solution. It is about taking a step back, understanding the problem, asking why, and then figuring out what actually needs to be done.
And along with the research itself, being consistent, punctual and organised can make a huge difference to the entire process.

title: Writing Papers
text:
This page sets out how we write papers in the lab. It is for students writing their first paper, for anyone reviewing a draft, and for AI agents that help with either. Writing is a skill, and like any skill it improves with deliberate practice. This page gives you something concrete to practise against.
Every rule comes with a before and after, and every example follows one paper. Pick the paper with the switch below, and the whole page changes with it: text, tables and figures. Four are our own published papers. For those, the after follows the published paper and its numbers, and the before is an invented first draft, the kind every paper starts as. Kestrel, the last one, is invented outright: it counts birds from cheap phone recordings, and its numbers are made up. Near the end, twenty real before-and-afters show how our published papers changed from first draft to print.
Kestrel counts birds from recordings made on cheap phones. It is invented, and so are its numbers.
Gemello estimates how much energy each appliance in a home uses, from just the monthly electricity bill. Paper
ThermEval asks whether vision-language models can read thermal images. Paper · project
JoulesEye estimates calories burned from breathing, seen by a phone's thermal camera. Paper
GD-MI decides where to put new air-quality sensors, by moving them all at once with gradient descent. Paper · project

title: Writing Papers
text:
Five principles
Every rule on this page comes from one of five principles.

Write for a smart reader from a neighbouring field. Picture a researcher who knows machine learning well but has never read a paper in your subfield. That reader should be able to follow every section.
State the point first. Every abstract line, paragraph, section and caption opens with its takeaway. The details follow.
Go from concrete to abstract. Show a small example with real numbers, and then give the general form.
Back every claim with evidence. Use a number, a table, a figure, a proof or a citation. If you cannot back a claim, narrow it until you can.
Be honest. Show your failures and limitations yourself, before a reviewer finds them. A reviewer trusts you more when you do.




The reader you write for knows the field next door. Your job is to build the bridge.

title: Writing Papers
text:
The skeleton: abstract, introduction, paper
I gave a talk on how to write a paper (recording, slides), and I recommend watching it. Other material from the talk is in the Research Methods Bootcamp repository. The core idea is simple: the abstract is the skeleton of the paper.
Write the abstract first. Each abstract line then grows into one paragraph of the introduction. Each paragraph then grows into one section of the paper.



One abstract line becomes one introduction paragraph, which becomes one section. The insight line is optional.


A quick test. Read only the first sentence of each introduction paragraph, in order. If those sentences read like your abstract, the structure works. If they don’t, fix the structure before you polish any sentence.

title: Writing Papers
text:
Title
A good title names the method and says what it does. Keep it short.



A Novel Deep Learning Framework for Robust Few-Shot Bioacoustic Species Classification Using Low-Cost Mobile Devices in Real-World Settings


Kestrel: Few-Shot Bird Counting from Cheap Phone Recordings






A Novel Data-Driven Approach for Scalable Non-Intrusive Appliance-Level Energy Estimation in Residential Buildings


Gemello: Creating a Detailed Energy Breakdown from just the Monthly Electricity Bill


The after says what you get (a breakdown) from what you already have (the monthly bill). Gemello is Italian for twin: the method finds each home’s twins among homes that are already metered.




Towards a Comprehensive Understanding of the Capabilities of State-of-the-Art Vision-Language Models on Thermal Images


ThermEval: A Structured Benchmark for Evaluation of Vision-Language Models on Thermal Imagery


The before hides the contribution behind “towards” and “comprehensive understanding”. The after names the benchmark first, so people can cite it in one word.




A Novel Smartphone-Based Deep Learning Approach for Accurate Calorie Estimation Using Thermal Data


JoulesEye: Energy Expenditure Estimation and Respiration Sensing from Thermal Imagery While Exercising


JoulesEye is a name people can say and remember: joules of energy, seen by an eye. The subtitle then names both outputs and the setting, while exercising, which is where watches fail.




An Efficient and Scalable Novel Framework for Optimal Sensor Placement in Air Quality Monitoring Networks


Scalable Air-Quality Sensor Placement via Gradient-Based Mutual Information Maximization


The after says what is new, gradient-based, instead of claiming efficient and novel. One step better: the paper calls its method GD-MI, so the title could lead with it, as in GD-MI: Scalable Air-Quality Sensor Placement via Gradient-Based Mutual Information.


Give the method a name people can say. A real word that fits the idea works best. If you build an acronym, make it spell out the subtitle.
Use no word the paper does not earn. Drop words like novel, robust and real-world unless the paper argues them explicitly.
Keep scoping words that are true. “Cheap phone recordings” is a promise you can keep. “Any audio” is not.
Put the name in a macro, so a late rename is a one-line change:


\newcommand{\method}{Gemello\xspace}   % needs \usepackage{xspace}


\newcommand{\method}{ThermEval\xspace}     % needs \usepackage{xspace}
\newcommand{\dataset}{ThermEval-D\xspace}  % the paper names its dataset separately


\newcommand{\method}{JoulesEye\xspace}   % needs \usepackage{xspace}


\newcommand{\method}{GD-MI\xspace}   % needs \usepackage{xspace}


\newcommand{\method}{Kestrel\xspace}   % needs \usepackage{xspace}

title: Writing Papers
text:
Abstract
We follow the structure from RM101: seven parts, plus an optional insight. Each part gets one line, so a full abstract is 7–8 lines. A line may hold two short sentences.









Part
What it says
Kestrel




1 Context
Where the field is
Bird counts tell ecologists how habitats change. Volunteers now record birdsong on cheap phones, at a scale no survey team can match.


2 Motivation
The problem
But phone audio is noisy, and most species have only a handful of labelled calls.


3 Prior art
Why existing work falls short
Existing classifiers need hundreds of clean calls per species. On phone audio, their accuracy drops from 91% to 54%.


4 Insight (optional)
What explains the gap
We find that the phone’s microphone, not the bird, causes most of this drop.


5 Approach
What we do
We present Kestrel, which learns to undo each phone’s microphone before it classifies a call. Kestrel needs only five labelled calls to add a new species.


6 Evaluation
How we test it
We test it on 12,000 clips from 40 phone models and 150 species, against six baselines.


7 Results
What we found, in numbers
Kestrel reaches 83% accuracy on phone audio, against 61% for the best baseline. That baseline needs a hundred labelled calls per species; Kestrel needs five.


8 Conclusion
What it means, and its limits
Cheap phones can thus support bird surveys at scale. Kestrel still fails on overlapping calls, which we leave to future work.



Here is the same content, written the way first drafts usually are, and then rewritten.


Bird population monitoring is an important problem in ecology which has received a lot of attention, and with the proliferation of low-cost smartphones it has become possible for large numbers of volunteers to record bird vocalisations, although the resulting recordings are noisy and labelled data for most species is scarce. Existing approaches, which are mostly based on deep convolutional networks trained on curated recordings, have been shown to perform well on clean audio, but it is observed that their accuracy degrades significantly when they are applied to recordings collected using phones. In this paper, a novel framework called Kestrel is proposed, in which the frequency response of each device is estimated and compensated before classification is performed, and a few-shot learning strategy is employed so that new species can be added with only a small number of labelled examples. Extensive experiments were conducted on a large dataset and it is shown that Kestrel significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, which demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach.


Bird counts tell ecologists how habitats change. Volunteers now record birdsong on cheap phones, at a scale no survey team can match. But phone audio is noisy, and most species have only a handful of labelled calls. Existing classifiers need hundreds of clean calls per species. On phone audio, their accuracy drops from 91% to 54%. We find that the phone’s microphone, not the bird, causes most of this drop. We present Kestrel, which learns to undo each phone’s microphone before it classifies a call. Kestrel needs only five labelled calls to add a new species. We test it on 12,000 clips from 40 phone models and 150 species, against six baselines. Kestrel reaches 83% accuracy on phone audio, against 61% for the best baseline. That baseline needs a hundred labelled calls per species; Kestrel needs five. Cheap phones can thus support bird surveys at scale. Kestrel still fails on overlapping calls, which we leave to future work.


The two versions are almost the same length. The second one says more. It gives the size of the drop, the insight, the data, the margin over the best baseline, and a limitation. The first one hides behind “significantly” and “extensive”.










Part
What it says
Gemello




1 Context
Where the field is
The first step to saving energy in a home is often an energy breakdown: how much each appliance uses, like an itemised grocery bill.


2 Motivation
The problem
But producing one needs hardware installed in every home, so it does not scale.


3 Prior art
Why existing work falls short
Disaggregation methods split a home’s total power into appliances, but they need high-frequency metering in each home.


4 Insight (optional)
What explains the gap
Homes in a region are alike, and “alike” can be defined per appliance: similar seasonal bills mean similar heating and cooling; similar floor area means similar lighting.


5 Approach
What we do
We present Gemello, which estimates a home’s breakdown from similar homes whose breakdown is known. It needs only the monthly bill and facts such as floor area and household size.


6 Evaluation
How we test it
We test it on 57 homes from the public Dataport data set, against two disaggregation methods that need metering in each home.


7 Results
What we found, in numbers
Gemello estimates heating and cooling energy with 76% accuracy, against 61% and 56% for the two baselines. With only seven metered homes to learn from, it still reaches about 69%.


8 Conclusion
What it means, and its limits
Its inputs already exist for most homes, so it could be used today. It gives monthly estimates only, and only for common appliances.



Here is a first draft of the same abstract, and the rewrite.


Energy conservation in residential buildings is an important research problem and has received significant attention from the research community. Appliance-level energy feedback has been shown to be useful, but existing non-intrusive load monitoring techniques suffer from several limitations which hinder their large-scale adoption. In this paper, a novel data-driven approach called Gemello is proposed, which leverages readily available data to estimate appliance-level energy consumption in a scalable manner. The proposed approach is evaluated on a real-world data set and the results demonstrate that it achieves promising performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques.


The first step to saving energy in a home is often an energy breakdown: how much each appliance uses. But producing one needs hardware installed in every home, so it does not scale. Disaggregation methods need high-frequency metering in each home. Homes in a region are alike, and “alike” can be defined per appliance. Similar seasonal bills mean similar heating and cooling; similar floor area means similar lighting. We present Gemello, which estimates a home’s breakdown from similar homes whose breakdown is known. It needs only the monthly bill and facts such as floor area and household size. We test it on 57 homes from the public Dataport data set, against two methods that need metering in each home. Gemello estimates heating and cooling energy with 76% accuracy, against 61% and 56% for the baselines. With only seven metered homes to learn from, it still reaches about 69%. Its inputs already exist for most homes, so it could be used today. It gives monthly estimates only, and only for common appliances.


The draft names no limitation of prior work: “several limitations which hinder their large-scale adoption” could mean anything. The rewrite names the one that matters, hardware in every home, and the whole paper answers it. The published paper is honest in another way worth copying: for the fridge, one baseline beats Gemello (72% against 69%), and the paper says so.










Part
What it says
ThermEval




1 Context
Where the field is
Vision-language models (VLMs) answer questions about ordinary photos well. Thermal cameras see heat instead of light, which matters at night, in search and rescue and in medical screening.


2 Motivation
The problem
But a thermal image encodes temperature, not colour or texture, and no benchmark tests whether VLMs can reason about it.


3 Prior art
Why existing work falls short

4 Insight (optional)
What shapes the design
Reading a temperature takes a chain of steps: recognise the modality, read the colour bar, then map pixels to degrees.


5 Approach
What we do

6 Evaluation
How we test it
We evaluate 25 VLMs, from 0.3B to over 200B parameters, against human annotators.

Here is a first draft of the same abstract, and the rewrite.


Vision-language models have recently attracted significant attention in the computer vision community and have been shown to achieve impressive performance on a wide variety of tasks. However, their capabilities on thermal imagery, which is an important modality for numerous applications, have not been comprehensively studied. In this paper, a novel and comprehensive benchmark called ThermEval is proposed, which consists of a large number of question-answer pairs spanning multiple tasks, along with a new dataset containing thermal images with temperature annotations. Extensive experiments are conducted on a wide range of state-of-the-art open-source and closed-source models, and it is observed that the models struggle significantly on several tasks. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed benchmark and provide valuable insights for future research in this important area.


Vision-language models (VLMs) answer questions about ordinary photos well. Thermal cameras see heat instead of light, which matters at night, in search and rescue and in medical screening. But a thermal image encodes temperature, not colour or texture, and no benchmark tests whether VLMs can reason about it. VLM benchmarks use RGB images, and thermal datasets release coloured pictures without the temperatures behind them. Reading a temperature takes a chain of steps: recognise the modality, read the colour bar, then map pixels to degrees. We present ThermEval, which tests each link with more than 70,000 questions across seven tasks. Its new dataset, ThermEval-D, has over 3,500 thermal images with per-pixel temperatures. We evaluate 25 VLMs, from 0.3B to over 200B parameters, against human annotators. Asked which of two people is warmer, the best model is right 74% of the time, against 84% for people. Models often answer from language priors, such as a textbook body temperature, instead of the pixels. Bigger models do not reliably do better, and fine-tuning helps only on some tasks. Thermal understanding needs its own evaluation.


The draft says “a large number of question-answer pairs”, “multiple tasks” and “a wide range of models”. Fitness tracking using wearable devices has become extremely popular in recent years, and estimation of calories burned is one of the most widely used features. However, it has been observed in the literature that such estimates can be inaccurate. In this work, a novel system named JoulesEye is proposed, which leverages thermal imaging along with advanced signal processing and deep learning techniques to estimate energy expenditure in an accurate manner. A user study was conducted with a number of participants performing different exercises, and it was found that the proposed system achieves significantly lower error than commercial devices. The results demonstrate the feasibility and great potential of thermal sensing for health monitoring applications.


Phones and watches measure heart rate well, and fitness apps use it to estimate calories burned. But these estimates can be wrong by over 40%, too far off for medical use. The draft never says why thermal imaging should work. The rewrite gives the reason in one line, breathing, and the reader can then follow everything after it. “Significantly lower error” becomes 5.8% against 37.6%.










Part
What it says
GD-MI




1 Context
Where the field is
Over 99% of the world’s people breathe air above WHO limits. India has about 500 official monitoring stations for 1.4 billion people.


2 Motivation
The problem
Each new station is expensive, so where we place the next ones matters.


3 Prior art
Why existing work falls short
Mutual information (MI) picks informative sites, but its cost grows with every candidate site it checks. Cheap heuristics scale, but they cluster sensors or place them redundantly.


4 Insight (optional)
What explains the gap
If sensor coordinates are continuous parameters, we can move all the new sensors at once by gradient descent, with no search over candidate sites.


5 Approach
What we do
We present GD-MI. Its runtime does not grow with the number of sensors or the size of the candidate grid.


6 Evaluation
How we test it
We test it on PM2.5 data across India, against random placement, the maximum-variance heuristic and greedy MI.


7 Results
What we found, in numbers
With 100 new sensors across India, GD-MI lowers the error (RMSE) by 4% compared with the maximum-variance heuristic. With nine new sensors in one state, it reaches 5.8, against 5.6 for greedy MI, which is feasible only at that smaller scale.


8 Conclusion
What it means, and its limits
Information-based placement becomes feasible at national scale. Gradient descent depends on where the sensors start, and can stop in a local minimum.

Air pollution is a major problem worldwide and monitoring it is very important. Sensor placement is a well-studied problem and many approaches have been proposed in the literature, including mutual information based approaches which are known to be computationally expensive. In this paper we propose a novel, efficient and scalable gradient-based framework for optimal sensor placement which leverages the power of differentiable optimization. Extensive experiments on a large real-world dataset show that our approach significantly outperforms the baselines while being much faster, demonstrating its effectiveness for real-world deployment.


Over 99% of the world’s people breathe air above WHO limits. India has about 500 official monitoring stations for 1.4 billion people, and each new station is expensive. So where we place the next ones matters. Mutual information (MI) picks informative sites, but its cost grows with every candidate site it checks. Cheap heuristics scale, but they cluster sensors or place them redundantly. We treat sensor coordinates as continuous parameters, so we can move all the new sensors at once by gradient descent. We call this GD-MI. Its runtime does not grow with the number of sensors or the size of the candidate grid. We test it on PM2.5 data across India, against random placement, the maximum-variance heuristic and greedy MI. With 100 new sensors, GD-MI lowers the error by 4% compared with the maximum-variance heuristic. With nine new sensors in one state, it reaches an RMSE of 5.8, against 5.6 for greedy MI, which is feasible only at that scale. Gradient descent depends on where the sensors start, and can stop in a local minimum.


The draft claims efficient, scalable and significantly outperforms, and backs none of them. The rewrite shows the honest comparison too: greedy MI is slightly more accurate (5.6 against 5.8), and GD-MI wins on scale. Reviewers trust a paper that says where its method loses. One thing even the published paper could add: it calls GD-MI “orders of magnitude faster”, but reports no runtime. Every reader will want that number.

Abstract rules

Keep sentences short. Most should run 10–20 words, and none should go past about 25.
Make every number comparative. Write “83%, against 61% for the best baseline”, never a bare “83%”.
Put the main limitation in the last line. It costs one clause and buys a lot of trust.
Update the abstract’s numbers after every new run. You write the abstract first, so update it last.
Expand an acronym only if the reader needs it, and only once.
Leave out filler like “In this paper”, “extensive experiments” and “demonstrates the effectiveness”.

title: Writing Papers
text:
Introduction
The introduction is the abstract, grown. Write one paragraph per abstract line, in the same order. Each paragraph has the same anatomy.




Each paragraph opens with a lead sentence that states its point, and ends with a bridge to the next paragraph.







Each paragraph opens with a lead sentence that states its point, and ends with a bridge to the next paragraph.

Each paragraph opens with a lead sentence that states its point, and ends with a bridge to the next paragraph.







Each paragraph opens with a lead sentence that states its point, and ends with a bridge to the next paragraph.



The lead sentence sets the tone. It states the point of the paragraph. If a reader skims only the lead sentences, they should still get the argument.



Bird monitoring has a long history. Early surveys relied on trained observers walking fixed routes, and later work introduced automated recorders…


Existing bird classifiers fail on phone audio. Trained on clean recordings, they reach 91% accuracy; on phone clips of the same calls, they reach 54%…






Energy conservation in buildings has been an active area of research for several decades, and a wide variety of techniques have been proposed…


Buildings use more than 30% of the world’s energy, and an energy breakdown, how much each appliance uses, is one of the best ways to cut it…






Thermal imaging has a long history. It was first developed for military night vision, and over the decades it has found uses in industry, medicine and many other fields…


We do not know whether vision-language models can read a thermal image. They describe ordinary photos well, but a thermal image encodes temperature, not colour or texture…






Wearable devices have become increasingly popular over the last decade, and millions of people now use them to track their health and fitness…


Smartwatch calorie estimates can be wrong by more than 40%. They estimate it from heart rate alone, and heart rate misses much of what the body is doing…






Air pollution has been widely studied over the past decades, and many methods for monitoring it have been proposed in the literature…


India has about 500 official air-quality stations for 1.4 billion people. New stations are expensive, so each one must go where it adds the most information…



The last sentence builds a bridge. It leads the reader into the next paragraph, so the paragraphs connect organically. A question works well just before the insight:

“So why does accuracy collapse on phones?” The next paragraph then opens with the answer: “We find that the microphone, not the bird, causes the drop.”


“So can we get a breakdown without installing anything in the home?” The next paragraph then opens with the answer: “Yes, if we borrow it from similar homes that are already metered.”


“So can a model trained on ordinary photos read temperature at all?” The next paragraph then opens with how we find out: “To answer this, we break thermal understanding into seven tasks, from easy to hard.”


“So what does the watch miss?” The next paragraph then opens with the answer: “It misses breathing, and a thermal camera can see every breath.”


“Mutual information picks good sites, so why isn’t it used at national scale?” The next paragraph then opens with the answer: “Because its cost grows with every candidate site it checks.”

More rules for the introduction:

Don’t use bold run-in heads like “Challenges.” or “Our approach.” The lead sentence does that job, and does it better.
State your goals once and reuse them. For example: Gemello must be as accurate as methods that need hardware in every home (G1), use only data that already exists (G2), and need few metered homes to learn from (G3).ThermEval must test each step towards reading temperature on its own (G1), and score temperature answers against measured values, not guesses (G2).JoulesEye must sense breathing while the user cycles or runs hard (G1), estimate calories burned more accurately than a smartwatch (G2), and work with a thermal camera small enough for a watch (G3).GD-MI must place sensors nearly as well as greedy MI (G1), at a cost that does not grow with the grid (G2), without clustering them (G3).Kestrel must be accurate on phone audio (G1) and need few labels per species (G2). The evaluation later answers G1 and G2 by name.
Include a results paragraph with the headline numbers. Many drafts skip it, and reviewers notice.
Keep the contributions short: three to five items, ideally in running prose.
Put the caveats at the end. Don’t list weaknesses before the reader knows the method.

title: Writing Papers
text:
Background and related work
These are two separate sections, and they do two different jobs. Background teaches what the reader needs in order to follow your method. Related work places your paper among other papers.

Background

Open with why the section exists: “We now describe what each kind of electricity meter records, because Gemello works from the coarsest one: the monthly bill.”“We now describe how a thermal camera turns temperatures into colours, because most ThermEval tasks ask a model to turn those colours back into temperatures.”“We now describe how the body burns energy and how breathing reflects it, because JoulesEye estimates calories burned from breathing alone.”“We now describe how a neural process predicts PM2.5 and how sure it is, because GD-MI places sensors to shrink that uncertainty.”“We now describe how phone microphones distort sound, because Kestrel must undo that distortion.”
Explain in plain words, with one picture or analogy. For example: the monthly bill is the total at the bottom of a grocery receipt; an energy breakdown is the itemised list above it.a thermal image is a map of temperatures painted with a colour key; the colour bar is the map’s legend, and a new colour map repaints the same map.heart rate is like an engine’s revs: two engines at the same revs can burn very different amounts of fuel, depending on their size.each sensor is a lamp in a dark room; uncertainty is the dark, and two lamps side by side light the same patch twice.a phone colours sound the way a tinted window colours light; each phone has its own tint.
Define every symbol the method uses later. Define each one once, here.
Define every term before you use it, most of all in the abstract and Figure 1, which are read first.
Anchor anything the reader may not know: a place, a dataset, an agency. “Madhya Pradesh, a central Indian state about the size of Germany” tells a reader abroad what “MP” does not.
End with the two or three facts the method builds on.
Add a figure if the mechanism is hard to picture.

Put background before related work whenever the way you group prior work depends on it.


Related work
The first sentence is always “We now categorize …”. It names the axis along which you group prior work. Pick an axis that matters for your contribution, such as what methods need, where they act or what they assume.
Then write one family per paragraph. Give each family a short run-in head, which is fine here. Open with a verdict, and end with one line on how you relate: what you share, how you differ, and what the difference buys.


We now categorize prior work by what it must install in each home.
Per-appliance and indirect sensing. Sensing systems give accurate breakdowns, but they need hardware in every home. Some put a sensor on each appliance [26, 16] or circuit [37]; others infer use from vibration, temperature or electrical noise [32, 25, 20]. Like them, Gemello learns from appliance-level measurements; unlike them, it needs those measurements in only a few homes, not all.
Non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM). NILM needs only one meter per home, but that meter must sample every minute or faster [39, 11]. Most smart meters record every 15 minutes or hourly, and most of the world has none. NILM also needs a model of each appliance, and such models have not been shown to transfer across homes [21, 33]. Like NILM, Gemello starts from a home’s total energy; unlike NILM, it needs one reading a month and no appliance models.




We now categorize prior work by whether it can score a temperature answer.
RGB benchmarks for VLMs. RGB benchmarks test perception and reasoning broadly, but only on ordinary photos. MME, MMBench, SEED-Bench and MM-Vet cover many tasks [21, 35, 36, 42, 58, 59], and newer benchmarks add adversarial and harder questions [37, 49]. Like them, ThermEval scores VLMs on visual questions; unlike them, its images encode temperature, where a plausible answer can still be wrong.
Thermal and multispectral benchmarks. These benchmarks do use thermal images, but they allow only fixed-choice answers. One builds multiple-choice questions with GPT-4o [15]; RGB-Th-Bench asks binary questions and never tests temperature reading [47]. Like them, ThermEval tests VLMs on thermal images; unlike them, it also asks for temperatures in degrees, scored against measured per-pixel values.




We now categorize prior work by what it can still sense while the user exercises.
Respiration sensing. Chest belts, RGB cameras and earables track breathing well at rest, but vigorous motion drowns the signal. A chest belt confuses pedalling with breathing, because both move the chest at a similar rate [31]. RGB methods amplify light flickering across a moving face [77], and earable methods were tested on everyday head movements [2]. Like them, JoulesEye needs no mask; unlike them, it sees warm and cool air at the nostrils, which room lighting does not affect.
Energy expenditure estimation. Wearables estimate calories from motion or heart rate, which is convenient but error prone. Accelerometer methods rely on predictive equations that vary widely [47], and heart-rate watches disagree from brand to brand [17]. Accurate alternatives need ECG probes across the torso [54] or confine one person to a room watched by a thermal camera [26, 38]. Like them, JoulesEye uses a sensor a watch can carry; unlike them, it adds breathing, which tracks calorie burn better than heart rate.




We now categorise prior work by how it searches for sites.
Greedy mutual information. Greedy MI picks sites one at a time, each the one that most reduces uncertainty over the map [3, 7]. Because MI is submodular, this greedy choice is provably near-optimal. But it must score every candidate site before each pick, and its Gaussian-process model scales cubically with the data [7, 12]. Like it, GD-MI scores placements by the uncertainty they remove; unlike it, GD-MI never scores each candidate site.
Learned placement policies. Neural processes learn from many past pollution maps and give uncertainty quickly on a new one [5, 9]. Placement methods built on them still pick sites one at a time from a discrete list, and that choice cannot be differentiated [2]. Like them, GD-MI uses a neural process for its uncertainty; unlike them, it moves all the new sensors at once, by gradient descent.




We now categorize prior work by what it needs to learn a new species.
Supervised classifiers. Supervised classifiers are accurate on clean audio, but they need hundreds of labelled calls per species. They train on curated recordings [3, 7] and degrade on phone audio [12]. Like them, Kestrel classifies calls with a neural network; unlike them, it needs five calls per species, not hundreds.
Denoising front-ends. Denoising front-ends clean the audio before any classifier sees it [5, 9]. They remove background noise, but they cannot remove the microphone’s own colouring, because that colouring is not noise. Like them, Kestrel fixes the audio before classification; unlike them, it models each phone, which is where most of the error comes from.



Group by idea, never by date. “Recent work” ages quickly, and it has no thread.
Use the same groups in your comparison table as in the text.
Every claim about another method must come from its paper or your own run. Say which.
Hedge every “first”. Write “to our knowledge, no prior work …”, and only after a real search. Cite only papers you have read.

A toy example teaches more than an equation. Use two dimensions and numbers small enough to check in your head. Follow the same toy through every step.


Suppose we want the lighting energy of home X, which has 1,500 sq ft. Three metered homes have 1,400, 1,600 and 3,000 sq ft. They use 20, 30 and 80 kWh a month on lights. For lighting, Gemello compares floor area, so X’s two nearest twins are the first two homes. It averages their lighting: (20 + 30) ÷ 2 = 25 kWh. For heating and cooling, it compares summer bills instead, so X may get different twins. Real homes have many features and many metered homes, but every step works the same way.




Suppose a colour bar runs from 30 °C (dark) to 40 °C (bright) in ten equal steps, so each step is 1 °C. Person A’s nose sits on step 4, so it is 34 °C. Person B’s nose sits on step 6, so it is 36 °C. B is hotter, and the camera’s stored temperatures confirm it. A model that reads 34 as 340 has broken the colour-bar link. A model that answers 37 °C for every nose has ignored the pixels. Each wrong answer points to a different broken link.




Suppose we watch the nostrils for 10 seconds. Their brightness rises and falls four times: warm air out, cool air in. So the breathing rate is 4 × 6 = 24 breaths a minute. The first model turns this rate into the volume of air breathed out. The second turns that volume into oxygen used, say 10 ml per kg per minute. For a 60 kg rider, that is 10 × 60 = 600 ml, or 0.6 litres, a minute. At 5 kcal per litre of oxygen, the rider burns 0.6 × 5 = 3 kcal a minute. Real models learn both steps from data, but the chain is the same.




Suppose the map has just two sites. Site A sits next to an existing station, so the model is fairly sure of it: uncertainty 1. Site B is far from any station: uncertainty 9. A new sensor at position x, from A (x = 0) to B (x = 1), clears the uncertainty near it. That leaves x + 9(1 − x) = 9 − 8x in total. We start the sensor at x = 0.25, which leaves 7. The gradient is −8, so moving towards B helps. One step of size 0.05 takes it to x = 0.65, which leaves 3.8. The next step would carry it past B, so we snap it to B, which leaves 1. Real maps have thousands of sites and many sensors, but every step works the same way.




Suppose sound has just two frequency bands, low and high. A bird sings with energy (4, 2). Phone A halves the high band, so it records (4, 1). From a few clips, Kestrel learns that phone A’s gain is (1, 0.5). It divides the gain out: (4, 1) ÷ (1, 0.5) = (4, 2). The bird’s song is back. Real audio has hundreds of bands, but every step works the same way.


More rules for the method:

Keep the method generic, with no exact counts. “We match each home to its nearest metered homes” belongs in the method. “57 homes from Dataport, with K from 1 to 6” belongs in the evaluation.“We test each model at several imaging distances” belongs in the method. “2 ft, 6 ft and 10 ft” belongs in the evaluation.“We track the nostrils in the thermal video” belongs in the method. “A FLIR One Pro at 8.6 frames per second” belongs in the evaluation.“We start from the existing stations and add k new sensors” belongs in the method. “Up to 100 new sensors, added to India’s CPCB network” belongs in the evaluation.“We record clips from several phones” belongs in the method. “40 phone models” belongs in the evaluation.
Use few equations: only the ones the reader needs to follow the argument. Move derivations and implementation details to the appendix.
Present textbook results as design guarantees, and name the parts that are truly new. Don’t list a textbook theorem as a contribution.
Keep notation clean. Never use one symbol for two things.
Verify every toy number in code before it goes into the paper.

Evaluation
Call the section Evaluation, and make it question-driven. A model I like is the evaluation of Gemello (KDD 2016). The reader can predict its skeleton: data, baselines, metric, then one experiment per question.

We now evaluate Gemello against the goals of Section 1. We ask:

Q3 (G3): How many metered homes does Gemello need to learn from?
Q4: Does 15-minute smart-meter data help, where a home has it?
Q5: What makes two homes similar, for each appliance?





We now use ThermEval to test 25 VLMs against the goals of Section 1. We ask:

Q3 (G2): Can they tell which person, or which body part, is hotter?
Q4 (G2): Can they estimate a temperature in degrees?
Q5: Do larger models, richer prompts or fine-tuning close the gap?





We now evaluate JoulesEye against the goals of Section 1. We ask:

Q2 (G2): Does it estimate calories burned more accurately than a smartwatch?
Q3 (G3): Does a 32×24-pixel thermal camera still work?
Q4: Which inputs matter most: breathing, heart rate or skin temperature?





We now evaluate GD-MI against the goals of Section 1. We ask:

Q1: Which model gives the most useful uncertainty to place sensors with?
Q2 (G1): How close does GD-MI come to greedy MI, in a region small enough for greedy MI to run?
Q3 (G1, G2): Across all of India, where greedy MI is too slow, does GD-MI beat the maximum-variance heuristic?

We now evaluate Kestrel against the goals of Section 1. We ask:

Q2 (G2): How few labelled calls does a new species need?
Q3: Does Kestrel work on phones it has never seen?
Q4: Which part of Kestrel matters most?
