Give every baseline its best chance. Tune all methods with the same rule. Use the authors’ code where you can. Check that your copy reproduces a published number.
Metrics, listed by goal. Define each one so the reader could recompute it, and say whether higher or lower is better.
Protocol. Give the number of seeds, the confidence intervals and the statistical tests.
Reproducibility. Say what you will release.

A new metric gets its own subsection inside Evaluation, not its own section. Open with the failure it fixes, using your own numbers. List each failure with its fix, and give the formula last.


Results
Make each subsection a question, and answer it in its first sentence.



4.5 Results. In this section, we present the results of our approach and the baselines. Figure 3 shows the energy accuracy of all methods…


4.5 From the monthly bill alone, is Gemello as accurate as methods that meter each home? Yes, and on HVAC it is more accurate: 76%, against 61% for FHMM and 56% for LBM (Figure 3). Only on the fridge does LBM lead, 72% against 69%…






5.4 Task 5: Thermal Reasoning. In this section, we evaluate the ability of VLMs to reason over thermal intensities. Table 4 shows the results of all models on the two subtasks…


5.4 Can VLMs tell which of two people is hotter? Not reliably. The best model, Gemini 3 Pro, is right 74% of the time, against 84% for people and 50% by chance (Table 4)…






6.2 Result on estimating energy expenditure. In this section, we present the results of energy expenditure estimation using different inputs. Figure 9 shows the MAPE of all the inputs…


6.2 Does JoulesEye estimate calories better than a smartwatch? Yes, by a wide margin: 5.8% error, against 37.6% for the Apple Watch’s own estimate (Figure 9)…






5.4 Results across India. In this section, we present the results of the large-scale experiment. Figure 2 shows the RMSE of all methods as a function of the number of added stations…


5.4 Does GD-MI beat the maximum-variance heuristic across India? Yes, and by more as the budget grows: with 100 new sensors, its RMSE is 7.1, against 7.4 for MaxVar (Figure 2)…






5.3 Results on unseen devices. In this section, we present results on devices not seen during training. Table 3 shows the accuracy of all methods…


5.3 Does Kestrel work on phones it has never seen? Yes, nearly as well: 79% on ten unseen phone models, against 83% on seen ones (Table 3)…



Give one headline figure that tells the main result at a glance. A trade-off plot with your method alone in the good corner beats any bar chart.




Gemello’s results drawn two ways. The bars need a legend and a careful read. The dot plot shows the message at once: from one meter reading a month, Gemello is the most accurate on heating and cooling, and close behind LBM on the fridge. Numbers from the paper’s text.







ThermEval’s Task 5 results drawn two ways. Twenty-four bars in alphabetical order hide the message. Against model size it is plain: open models from 0.3B to 235B parameters scatter around chance, and even the best model stays below people. Numbers from Table 4.







JoulesEye’s calorie errors drawn two ways. Coded bars send the reader to a legend. Sorted and labelled, the message is plain: every input with breathing stays under 6% error, against 10–12% for heart rate and 37.6% for the watch’s own estimate. Numbers from Figure 9.







GD-MI’s results drawn two ways. The bars hide that greedy MI was never run across India. The dot plot says it: GD-MI comes close to greedy MI where MI can run, and beats the maximum-variance heuristic at national scale. Numbers from the paper’s text.







The same invented results drawn two ways. The bar chart needs a legend and a careful read. The trade-off plot shows the message at once: Kestrel is alone in the good corner.




Explain why each baseline family fails, in one bullet each. Numbers alone do not convince.
Use an oracle or upper bound to separate the parts of your method. For example: with a perfect choice of twins, the paper’s Oracle beats Gemello on every appliance, so finding similar homes, not averaging them, limits accuracy.fine-tuning Qwen-VL 2.5 (8B) doubles its body-part ranking accuracy, from 0.32 to 0.64, but leaves two-person accuracy at 0.60, against 0.84 for people.even perfect heart rate leaves 10.2% error, against 5.8% for estimated breathing. Perfect breathing reaches 5.0%, so the signal matters more than sensing it perfectly.with nine new sensors, slow greedy MI reaches an RMSE of 5.6 and MaxVar 6.3; GD-MI, at 5.8, closes most of that gap.with perfect phone labels, accuracy rises only from 83% to 85%, so phone detection is not the bottleneck.
Choose sensitivity analyses that answer real questions, such as “how many metered homes does Gemello need to learn from?”“does the temperature error grow as the camera moves from 2 ft to 10 ft away?”“how many seconds of breathing does one estimate need?”“how does the gain over the heuristic change as the budget grows from 10 to 100 new sensors?”“how many labelled calls does a new species need?”.
Report effect sizes with intervals, not only p-values. For zero events, use the rule of three: 0 errors in 1,000 trials means an error rate of at most about 0.3%, at 95% confidence.
Show failure cases, with their causes.

title: Writing Papers
text:
Analysis, limitations and conclusion
Analysis asks “Why does it work?”. Write one question per design choice, in method order, each answered in its first sentence. Show both sides of every choice: too little fails, too much hurts, and there is a sweet spot. Admit what you cannot explain.
Limitations come as a numbered list. Each item has an italic verdict, the evidence, and a way forward.



Gemello gives monthly totals, not a power trace. It averages its twins’ monthly energy, so it cannot serve uses that need the trace, such as activity recognition or anomaly detection. Where a home has a smart meter, adding Gemello’s features to a trace-level method such as LBM is a natural next step.






Even after fine-tuning, temperature errors are too large for safety-critical use. The fine-tuned Qwen-VL 2.5 still misses absolute temperatures by 1–2 °C on T6 and T7. Its region error falls only from 2.85 °C to 2.60 °C. Pretraining that includes physical sensor data, not only RGB photos, is a natural next step.






The watch prototype is too slow for running. Its camera runs at 3 frames per second, so its breathing error is 8.1%, against 2.1% for the phone camera. Alone, its calorie error is 15.4%, worse than heart rate’s 12%; with heart rate, it is 10.1%. A faster low-resolution camera is the natural next step.






GD-MI can stop in a poor local minimum. Gradient descent depends on where the sensors start, so results vary from run to run. Figures 1 and 2 show the spread over five random starts. Running several starts, or starting from the heuristic’s placement, is a natural next step.






Kestrel fails on overlapping calls. When two species sing at once, accuracy falls to 41%. Source separation before classification is a natural next step.



The conclusion mirrors the abstract’s last lines in four to six sentences: problem, insight, method, headline numbers, takeaway. Two sentences are too few.

title: Writing Papers
text:
Sentences

Active voice
Use the active voice, with “we” for what you did. Active sentences are shorter. They also make clear who did what.








Passive
Active




It is observed that FHMM performs poorly on the dryer.
FHMM performs poorly on the dryer.


Experiments were conducted on 57 homes.
We test Gemello on 57 homes.


A novel approach, Gemello, is proposed.
We present Gemello.


Lighting energy is estimated from homes of similar area.
Gemello estimates lighting energy from homes of similar area.












Passive
Active




It is observed that complex colour maps lead to more failures.
Colour maps such as Summer and Spring cause more errors.


Experiments were conducted on 25 VLMs.
We evaluate 25 VLMs.


A novel benchmark, ThermEval, is proposed.
We present ThermEval.


Model outputs are parsed by a language model.
A text-only LLM parses each model’s answer.












Passive
Active




It has been observed that calorie estimates from wearables are inaccurate.
Wearable calorie estimates can be wrong by over 40%.


Experiments were conducted on 54 participants.
We test JoulesEye on 54 participants.


A novel system, JoulesEye, is proposed.
We present JoulesEye.


The nostril region is tracked across frames.
JoulesEye tracks the nostrils across frames.












Passive
Active




It is observed that MaxVar clusters sensors.
MaxVar clusters sensors.


Experiments were conducted on PM2.5 data across India.
We test GD-MI on PM2.5 data across India.


A novel gradient-based framework is proposed.
We present GD-MI.


The sensor coordinates are updated with Adam.
GD-MI updates the sensor coordinates with Adam.












Passive
Active




It is observed that accuracy drops on phones.
Accuracy drops on phones.


Experiments were conducted on 12,000 clips.
We test Kestrel on 12,000 clips.


A novel framework, Kestrel, is proposed.
We present Kestrel.


The gain is estimated from a few clips.
Kestrel estimates the gain from a few clips.




The passive is fine when the actor doesn’t matter: “The appliance data were recorded at one-minute resolution.”“All images were captured with a TOPDON TC001 Plus thermal camera.”“The data were collected in December and January, in a room kept at 76 °F.”“The PM2.5 maps were built from satellite, chemical-model and ground data, on a 0.1° grid.”“The clips were recorded between 2019 and 2023.”


Short sentences
Aim for a median of about 15–18 words and a maximum of about 25. Split any sentence with three or more clauses. Give each sentence one idea. The sentence-length figure shows what this does to an abstract.


Emphasis
Use \emph{} on the few words that carry the argument: every, only, not, before. Use it for contrast and for new terms. Don’t use it for decoration. One or two per paragraph is plenty.


NILM needs a meter reading every minute; Gemello needs one a month. It defines similarity per appliance, not per home.




Most VLMs can find the colour bar, but several cannot read it. A thermal image encodes temperature, not colour or texture.




A chest belt cannot tell breathing from pedalling, because both move the chest at a similar rate. JoulesEye watches the nostrils, not the chest.




Greedy MI must score every candidate site before it places each sensor. GD-MI moves all the new sensors at once, so a finer grid adds no extra search.




Denoising removes background noise, but it cannot remove the microphone’s colouring. Kestrel models each phone, not each recording.




Cut the filler







Instead of
Write




In this paper, we propose
We present


It is worth noting that X
X


The intuition is simple: X
X


a novel / crucial / groundbreaking method
a method (show why it matters)


comparable to or better thansignificantly below human performancesignificantly bettersignificantly bettersignificantly better
76% vs 61% and 56% on HVAC; 69% vs 72% on the fridge, where LBM wins74% vs 84% (and the test, if you mean statistical significance)5.8% vs 37.6% error (MAPE) for the Apple Watch’s own estimateRMSE of 7.1 against 7.4 for MaxVar with 100 new sensors, 4% lower (and the test, if you mean statistical significance)83% vs 61% (and the test, if you mean statistical significance)


due to the fact that
because



Write like a person. Avoid inflated words, stacked hedges (“may potentially suggest”) and three-item lists that are only there for rhythm.


Numbers and terms

Never write a bare number. Compare it to something, and give its unit and its n.
Compare rates, not counts, when the totals differ. “20 of 40 (50%) became 15 of 20 (75%)” is a rise, though 20 → 15 looks like a fall.
Describe what you did, not a verdict on it. Don’t write validated, established or confirmed unless the paper shows that test.
Without a causal design, write “we observe” and “is associated with”, not “caused” or “impact”. If an interval includes zero, say so in the same sentence.
Every adjective needs a number. Low-overhead, real-time and scalable each need a latency, a memory or a size.
Use one word per concept. If you call them metered homes, don’t switch to submetered, train, instrumented and neighbourhood homes later.If you call it a colour bar, don’t switch to colorbar, temperature scale and legend later.If you call it energy expenditure, don’t switch to calorie burn, caloric expenditure and VO2 later.If you call TNP-D the surrogate, don’t switch to predictive model, the NP and the model later.If you call it a gain, don’t switch to response, profile and filter later.
Expand an acronym once, and only if you use it again.



American and British English
Some spellings differ: British “colour” and “optimise” are American “color” and “optimize”. There are also a few differences in grammar. Pick one variety and stick to it. Most of our previous papers use British English, though this often depends on the co-authors.

title: Writing Papers
text:
Figures

One message, and a self-contained caption
Give each figure one message, and make that message the first sentence of the caption. A reader who sees only the figure and its caption should understand it.



Figure 3. Energy accuracy of different approaches across appliances.


Figure 3. From the monthly bill alone, Gemello is as accurate as methods that meter each home. Each group is one appliance; bars give energy accuracy (%, higher is better) for FHMM, LBM and Gemello, with standard errors across homes. LBM leads on the fridge, 72% to 69%.






Figure 2. Overview of the tasks in the ThermEval benchmark.


Figure 2. ThermEval asks seven kinds of question, each one step closer to reading temperature. From left: is it thermal (T1–T2), how many people (T3), what the colour bar says (T4), who is hotter (T5) and how hot (T6–T7). Each panel shows one real question from the benchmark.






Figure 9. MAPE of energy expenditure estimation for different inputs.


Figure 9. Breathing predicts calories burned far better than heart rate. Error (MAPE, lower is better) of each input’s calorie estimate against an indirect calorimeter. Every input with breathing (RR) stays under 6%; heart rate alone gives 10–12%, and the Apple Watch’s own estimate 37.6%.






Figure 1. Results of different methods on the regional subset.


Figure 1. With nine new sensors, GD-MI nearly matches greedy MI and beats MaxVar. Validation RMSE in Madhya Pradesh (lower is better) as 0 to 9 sensors join the existing CPCB stations. Bands show the 25th to 75th percentile over five runs of the two random methods, GD-MI and Random.






Figure 4. Results of different methods on the phone dataset.


Figure 4. Kestrel is the only method that is both accurate and label-efficient. Each point is one method: accuracy on phone audio (x) against labelled calls needed per species (y, log scale). The shaded corner is the goal.



If a figure needs a paragraph to decode, split it into step-by-step panels with one idea per panel, or move the detailed version to the appendix.


Colour that means something
Use one colour code for the whole paper. Give each colour a meaning, and state the code once. Show movement or change as a colour change: the problem starts orange, your method’s blue arrow moves it, and it lands green.



Colour as meaning. On the left the colours are arbitrary, so the reader needs a legend. On the right the same code holds across the whole paper.



Use a colour-blind-safe palette. Okabe–Ito is a good default.
Never let meaning depend on colour alone. Add ✓/✗, filled and hollow markers, or direct labels.
Give neutral categories neutral colours, so they never clash with the semantic code.
Keep text at least 6–7 pt at final size. Check the rendered PDF for overlaps, clipping and margin overflow.
Read every plotted number from your results files, not from memory.
Check each plot’s shape against your analysis. A straight line on a log-y axis means exponential growth; if your theory says polynomial, the axis or the data is wrong.
Every image comes from the run it claims to show. Label an illustration as one, and never submit a generated mock-up as a photo of your setup.



LaTeXify figures
Use our LaTeXify Python package to turn matplotlib figures into publication-ready plots. See our local guide for installation and examples. It gives you three things:

Precise figure sizing. Figures are sized relative to the column or page width, so you rarely need manual sizing inside \begin{figure}.
Font size control. Font size is set relative to the document’s text size, so labels stay readable.
LaTeX font matching. Figures use LaTeX fonts, so they match the rest of the document.


Tip: You can find the page width and column width with \the\textwidth and \the\columnwidth.

title: Writing Papers
Writing Papers
text:
LaTeX hygiene

Use \cref for every reference. Never hand-type “Figure 3” or “Table S2”. This includes references into the supplement: load xr-hyper, add \externaldocument[S-]{supp}, and write \cref{S-tab:ablation}. On Overleaf, add a latexmkrc file so that the supplement is compiled too.
Use macros for the method name, metric names and recurring symbols.
Keep a label scheme: sec:, fig:, tab:, eq:.
Write one sentence per source line. Diffs and reviews become much easier.


Comments in LaTeX
We create a comment macro for each author’s initials (I use \nb). Comments are useful for notes on the text, and for notes to yourself. I might write \nb{I'm not sure about this sentence}, and later search for every \nb to find my comments. Put all notes behind one switch, so the submission build hides them:
\newif\ifshownotes \shownotestrue   % \shownotesfalse for submission
\newcommand{\nb}[1]{\ifshownotes{\color{red}\small\textbf{Nipun:} #1}\fi}
A separate submission.tex that sets \shownotesfalse and then inputs the paper makes this a one-click switch.

title: Writing Papers
text:
Reviewing a draft



Review in two layers: comments that explain why, and a suggested rewrite next to the original.


When you review someone’s draft, whether you are a student, an adviser or an AI agent, use the same protocol:

Don’t overwrite the author’s text. Add inline comments, and put a suggested rewrite after the original, behind the notes switch. The author decides what to keep.
Comment on the why, not just the what. “The lead sentence is history, so it doesn’t set the tone; lead with the claim” teaches. “Rewrite this” doesn’t.
Check every number you move or rephrase against its source table, figure or code. Rewriting can silently change a claim, such as “all 10” becoming “7 of 10”.
Mark anything you inferred with a “please check” note.
End with a short review guide: what changed and where, which runs are still needed, and which facts the author should confirm.

The next section shows this protocol at work on our own papers.

title: Writing Papers
section: How our published papers got better
text:
How our published papers got better
These are real drafts of our own published papers, taken from their Overleaf history. The before is an earlier version and the after is the published text, both cut to the sentences that show the point. Comments are quoted as the adviser or a co-author wrote them, with only typos fixed.

Titles and abstracts
Say how the method works, not that it is fast. GD-MI, AAAI 2026


Fast and Scalable Sensor Placement for Air Quality Monitoring


Scalable Air-Quality Sensor Placement via Gradient-Based Mutual Information Maximization


Say why the problem matters first. Then give findings, not a list of contributions. ThermEval, KDD 2026


Images of different modalities possess unique characteristics that define their utility across various domains. … This paper introduces ThermEval, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate the zero-shot performance of VLMs on thermal imagery… ThermEval makes three key contributions: (1) identification of critical gaps in VLMs’ understanding of thermal imagery characteristics, (2) a structured evaluation framework for thermal-specific reasoning capabilities, and (3) a novel dataset…


Thermal sensing plays a critical role in settings where visible spectrum fails, including night-time surveillance, search & rescue, autonomous driving, and medical screening. … Evaluating 25 open-source and closed-source VLMs, we find that models consistently fail at temperature-grounded reasoning, degrade under colormap transformations, and default to language priors or fixed responses, with only marginal gains from prompting or supervised fine-tuning.



you have to motivate the need/importance of thermal imagery before
Can you try and remove 1-3 not so useful sentences and get 1-3 lines instead of insights? like: language priors, etc.. 4-5 such points in abstract would be good.

Don’t stop the abstract at the method. Give the results, with numbers. FlowSat, BMVC 2026


…yet existing generative foundation models inherit dated architectural choices from natural-image diffusion. We present FlowSat, the first Diffusion Transformer (DiT) trained with flow matching for satellite imagery that conditions on the geographic and acquisition metadata intrinsic to remote-sensing data… FlowSat fine-tunes from a large pretrained text-to-image DiT backbone … so that metadata modulates the network at the global semantic level rather than as pixel-grade input channels.


…yet existing models inherit slow denoising U-Nets from natural-image diffusion and treat acquisition metadata weakly… On fMoW-RGB, FlowSat attains the best FID and CLIP score among compared methods in only 20 Euler steps, at least 2.5× fewer than competing diffusion baselines. An encoder-controlled ablation attributes the gain to the geometry-aware encoding itself, improving FID from 46.81 to 37.96 with roughly 11× fewer conditioning parameters than a plain sinusoidal encoder.




Introductions
Go concrete. Open with one real question that people cannot yet answer. VayuBench, CODS 2025


Our focus on open-source models serves several important purposes: …
Q1: How can we evaluate LLM performance on complex and specialized air pollution related data analysis tasks?


Even seemingly simple questions such as ‘How did PM2.5 levels change in Delhi last year?’ remain difficult for most stakeholders to answer directly. …
Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for translating natural-language requests into executable analyses, offering the potential to make environmental data as accessible as a search query.


End the introduction with your results, not with the last task. ThermEval, KDD 2026


T6 Activity Classification: Evaluates high-level semantic reasoning by requiring models to infer human activities (e.g., sleeping, walking, sitting) based solely on thermal postures and heat distribution patterns, without relying on visual appearance cues.


We evaluate 25 VLMs ranging from 0.3B to over 200B parameters, spanning both open-source and closed-source families… While most VLMs reliably distinguish raw thermal from RGB images, performance degrades sharply on tasks requiring temperature reasoning or estimation. … These failure modes appear across model scales, indicating that the limitation lies in cross-modal grounding rather than model size. … This work makes the following contributions:



the intro ends suddenly..
can we break into 2 paras – first one on method, evaluation; next one on insights. We can expand insights by 2-3 lines.

Make each contribution a claim that points to its evidence. SentinelKilnDB, NeurIPS 2025


We envision SentinelKilnDB being used for the following research directions: … Oriented object detection in low-resolution, multi-spectral imagery with fine-grained class separation.



We introduce SentinelKilnDB, a Sentinel-2 benchmark containing bounding boxes of 62,671 brick kilns across South Asia … (see Section …).
We provide a benchmark of 28 state-of-the-art object detection models developed over the past decade … (see Table …).
We show that pre-training remote sensing foundation models on satellite imagery yields significant gains over prior models … (see Table …).




Let’s highlight our contributions in bullet points as per the recent trend.



Related work
Open with a road map. Then, for each category: what exists, why it is not enough, what you do. ThermEval, KDD 2026


…However, these benchmarks remain RGB-centric and do not assess performance across alternative modalities.
Thermal and Other Multi-Spectral Benchmarks. Multispectral benchmarks highlight that different modalities encode distinct physical properties: thermal images capture temperature, depth images measure distance, and X-rays reveal internal structures. Thermal imagery is particularly relevant in safety-critical and low-visibility settings.


…We organize related work into three categories. First, we review benchmarks developed for thermal and multispectral modalities. Second, we survey existing thermal and infrared datasets. Finally, we discuss common evaluation practices…
Thermal and Multi-Spectral Benchmarks. Existing benchmarks provide limited evaluation of the reasoning required for thermal understanding. … In contrast, ThermEval targets thermal-specific challenges through structured tasks that require temperature reasoning and numerical estimation.



we now categorize related work …

Credit what prior work did. Then name what is still missing. NILMBench, BuildSys 2026


While foundational tools like the Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring Toolkit (NILMTK) have solved key issues related to data and metric standardization, new critical gaps have emerged. … Most modern comparisons remain computationally blind, ignoring efficiency metrics like inference time, FLOPs, and parameters. Prior work has focused on improving/benchmarking a few models rather than doing an extensive analysis of many models.


Despite this rapid innovation, reproducibly comparing diverse NILM models remains a significant challenge. Foundational toolkits such as NILMTK standardized datasets and pipelines, yet recent model comparisons emphasize accuracy, overlooking compute-efficiency metrics like FLOPs, parameters, and inference time. Moreover, evaluations typically focus on a single temporal resolution, limiting applicability across real-world use cases…

Say why prior work falls short, by its mechanism. “Expensive” is not a reason. GD-MI, AAAI 2026


A greedy naive placement of sensors based on maximum uncertainty fails to account for interaction effects between sensor locations and can lead to suboptimal joint configurations.


Principled methods grounded in information theory, such as maximizing mutual information (MI) between selected sensors and the unobserved field, can yield high-quality placements. However, MI-based acquisition requires a look-ahead evaluation at each candidate site to estimate potential information gain, making its runtime scale linearly with the number of candidates…

Claims the evidence can carry
Cite what you claim, and use the right word. ThermEval, KDD 2026


Concurrently, large-scale vision-language models (VLMs) such as LLaMA, LLaVA, Qwen-VL, and many others have redefined the landscape of multimodal AI. … Yet, their efficacy on out-of-distribution (OOD) modalities like thermal imagery remains largely unexamined.


VLMs achieve strong performance on RGB, even without task-specific training, as evidenced by numerous benchmarks evaluating their capabilities across diverse RGB-centric tasks. However, it is not clear whether these models can generalize to thermal imagery. This leads to an important question: Can VLMs trained predominantly on RGB data reason effectively about temperature-specific tasks in thermal images?

citations to prove this?

Second, and more critically, our cross-building evaluation uncovers a systemic failure to generalize, a fundamental limitation in the current state of the art. We demonstrate that even top-performing models are effective interpolators but poor extrapolators, consistently failing to disaggregate power levels and temporal signatures that fall outside their training distribution.

Strong correlation: Years with higher wind speeds (2019, 2020) had relatively lower PM2.5 concentrations

Justify every choice
Give a reason for every number you chose. VayuBench, CODS 2025


We generate n = 5 code samples for each query.


For each query, we sample n = 5 completions using temperature sampling (temperature = 0.8, top-p = 0.95). Prior work (e.g., …) often uses n = 20–100, but this is computationally prohibitive for our large dataset and multi-model comparison. Say where your categories came from. VayuBench, CODS 2025


Percentage distribution of each query category across the 5000 queries included in VayuBench. Category abbreviations defined in Section …


Guided by these goals, we drafted 65 seed questions across seven categories, all rooted in realistic policy and research scenarios. … A structured survey of policymakers, analysts, and practitioners rated the importance of each category (1–5 scale), suggested missing query types, and provided real-world examples.

Justify each split before a reviewer asks. NILMBench, BuildSys 2026


T1: Intra-Building Generalization. … UK-DALE, REDD, REFIT: Train on 30 days from Building 1; test on a held-out 1 week.
T2: … UK-DALE: Train on B1, B2; test on B4. REDD: Train on B1, B2, B3; test on B6. REFIT: Train on B2, B3; test on B4.

While cross-validation is generally preferred, we use a static split for Task T2 because the buildings in our dataset have disjoint temporal coverage.

Results and captions
Describe what a model does, not what it assumes. ThermEval, KDD 2026


PaliGemma, in particular, always assumes RGB input, yielding fixed accuracies of 0.5 for Task 1 and 0 for Task 2.


Notably, BLIP-2 consistently predicts all inputs as thermal images, which leads to poor performance on the tasks.



how do we know it assumes RGB? I would tone down, cut this sentence

Define every mark in a table in its caption. SentinelKilnDB, NeurIPS 2025


Comparison of oriented object detection methods across categories, including backbone, bounding box type (AA: Axis-Aligned, OBB: Oriented), overall mean Average Precision (mAP), and per-class mAP for CFCBK, FCBK, and Zigzag kiln types.


… The CA mAP50 refers to the class-agnostic mAP value, while CFCBK, FCBK, and Zigzag indicate class-wise AP50 scores. In the table, we mark the highest score in bold and underline the second-highest score in each column.

Paper timelines
Plan backwards from the deadline. The schedule below is a starting point; adjust it to the venue and the project.



A suggested eight-week plan. Writing starts while experiments run, results freeze three weeks out, and the last week is for checks, not new content.



Write the abstract and sketch the figures in week one. They tell you which experiments you still need.
Freeze results about three weeks before the deadline. After that, write; don’t run.
Book an internal review: your adviser and one peer who is not on the paper. The peer is your “reader from a neighbouring field”.

title: Writing Papers
text:
Grammarly, AI tools and agents
I recommend that students use Grammarly (or a similar tool) to check their writing, once they have done a complete pass of editing. I do not recommend relying heavily on ChatGPT-like tools to write papers. They often produce sentences that sound correct but are not.
AI agents are most useful as reviewers and checkers, not as authors. They can flag long sentences, passive voice, hand-typed references and numbers that disagree with a table. They should never invent a number or a citation. You remain responsible for every claim.

The paper-writing skill
This guide also ships as an agent skill: a folder of instructions that an agent loads when it writes or reviews a paper. It lives in its own repository, sustainability-lab/paper-writing, and holds three files:

SKILL.md: the entry point, with the workflow and the core rules.
reference.md: every rule, section by section.
checklist.md: the pre-submission checklist.

Claude Code. Install it as a plugin, once, for all your projects:
/plugin marketplace add sustainability-lab/paper-writing
/plugin install paper-writing@sustainability-lab
Then ask: “Review the introduction of main.tex using the paper-writing skill.”
Other agents (Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor). Copy the repository’s skills/paper-writing/ folder into your paper’s repository, for example as docs/writing/. Then add one line to the project’s AGENTS.md or GEMINI.md: “When writing or reviewing the paper, follow docs/writing/SKILL.md.”
To change a rule, open a pull request on the repository, and update this page too, so that the two stay in step.

title: Writing Papers
text:
Pre-submission checklist

The abstract has 7–8 parts, short sentences, and the main limitation in its last line.
The introduction’s lead sentences, read in order, give the abstract.
Every paragraph opens with its point, and the introduction has no bold run-in heads.
Background and related work are separate. Related work opens with “We now categorize”, and each family ends with how we relate.
The method gives the intuition first, follows a toy example, and contains no experiment counts.
The evaluation goes from questions, to setup, to answer-first results, with one headline figure.
Every baseline got its best chance, and no headline cell is empty.
Every number in the text matches its table or figure.
Every reference uses \cref, including references to the supplement.
All figures share one colour code, are colour-blind safe, and have text of at least 6–7 pt.
No symbol stands for two things.
The limitations form a numbered list with ways forward, and the conclusion runs 4–6 sentences.
Page limit and anonymity are checked, and all notes are off in the submission build.

import latexify
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Configure for your document layout
latexify.latexify(columns=1)  # or columns=2 for double-column

# Create your plot as usual
x = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 100)

plt.plot(x, np.cos(x), label=r'$\cos(x)$')

latexify.format_axes(plt.gca())
latexify.save_fig('plot.pdf')

title: From Visualizations to Real-World Impact: My Journey at the Sustainability Lab
text:
About Me
Hi! I’m Vannsh Jani. I will be graduating with a B.Tech degree in Computer Science and Engineering in 2026. I had the incredible opportunity to work at the Sustainability Lab for a year during my sophomore year, and looking back, it completely reshaped who I am as a person and as a researcher.
When I first joined, my initial task was working on a project focused on Machine Learning visualizations. I was tasked with creating blogs and interactive applications to visualize core mathematical concepts behind ML. While it wasn’t direct academic research yet, this project forced me to build rock-solid fundamentals. It taught me my very first lesson about the lab: Prof. Nipun Batra values your commitment, curiosity, and passion to learn far more than what you already know on day one.


My Views
Working with Nipun Sir has been one of the defining experiences of my undergraduate life. The amount of time and energy he invests in guiding his students (both within academics and in life or career planning in general) is commendable.
I’ve experienced firsthand his absolute dedication to his students’ growth. Whenever we wrote papers, he would meticulously review our work across countless iterations, providing detailed, constructive feedback every single time. Even long after my formal tenure at the lab ended, Sir continued to offer his support, mentorship, and invaluable guidance when I was navigating my master’s applications. I will always remain deeply grateful for his constant presence as a mentor.


Research That Leaves the Lab
After the visualizations project, I stepped into actual computer vision research, working on detecting brick kilns from satellite imagery. This project was a massive eye-opener for me regarding how real-world research operates.

One of the most fulfilling feelings as an undergrad was realizing that the work we do here actually leaves the lab. Over time, I’ve received unexpected emails from people outside the institute using the live brick kiln detection web app I helped build. Knowing that your code and research are actively being utilized by others in the real world is an incredibly empowering feeling.

Our efforts eventually led to a research poster being accepted at ACM COMPASS 2024, which we traveled to present in-person in Delhi.



Sustainability Lab team at ACM COMPASS 2024




Overcoming the Initial Intimidation
I’ll be honest, when I started doing research, I felt heavily intimidated. I was just a second-year undergraduate surrounded by senior undergrads, experienced Master’s students like Suraj and Shataxi, and brilliant PhD candidates like Zeel and Rishabh. I worried that my ideas wouldn’t measure up.
However, the lab culture completely shattered that fear. The environment is structured so beautifully that everyone is encouraged to speak up, pitch ideas, and brainstorm together, regardless of whether you are the first author or the youngest person in the room. Working alongside Rishabh, Zeel, and the rest of the team taught me how to approach problems from absolute fundamentals and constantly question our underlying assumptions.


Values Learnt
Beyond coding and writing papers, the Sustainability Lab teaches you resilience. I vividly remember how hard Sir encouraged us to work during paper rebuttals. We would grind through multiple iterations to improve our work. Even when a paper didn’t get accepted immediately, that rigorous process significantly boosted our ratings and refined the work, giving it a much stronger foundation for its next submission. It taught me that rejections aren’t dead ends, they are just iterations toward a better version.
My time at the Sustainability Lab sparked a deep, lasting passion for Computer Vision and generative modeling, ultimately driving me to pursue a full-time research career. To anyone considering joining: if you are willing to show up, work hard, and stay curious, this lab will give you the wings to go anywhere you want.

title: From Beginner to Data Scientist: My Journey at Sustainability Lab
text:
I am R Yeeshu Dhurandhar, an alumnus of IIT Gandhinagar. I graduated in 2024 with majors in Electrical Engineering and dual minors in CSE and AI. Currently, I am working as a Data Scientist at Skan.AI. This narrative shares my enriching journey with Prof. Nipun Batra and the Sustainability Lab, which transformed me and provided me with a deep understanding of ML.


My journey with Prof. Batra began in my sixth semester with the Machine Learning course. Prior to this, my exposure to ML was minimal, but I was eager to dive into this fascinating domain, and this course helped with this. Prof. Batra’s teaching style is incredibly engaging. He has a knack for using precise terminology and encourages students to think critically. Each slide in his lectures is crafted to prompt the next step of thinking, fostering an environment where students are continually engaged. I particularly cherished the after-class discussions, where we delved into thought-provoking questions with him. The assignments and projects in his courses were rigorous and immensely educational. They provided a solid foundation and deep understanding of the subject matter.



In my seventh semester, I enrolled in the Probabilistic Machine Learning course and a project course under Prof. Batra. Initially, I had little research experience and was new to the topic we were exploring. However, this project course proved to be an excellent starting point for beginners like me. We had initial discussions about the project and assigned some tasks for the next week. I remember that our team met two days before the actual meeting with sir. That was the time when I realized that research can not be done at the last moment. It requires time to internalize things. Post this learning, I distributed the work over the week and things went well. In those days, we used to have long discussions in his office, during which we tried to understand conformal prediction deeply. Those discussions gave multiple new ideas on different directions for the research and provided a true essence of how the research happens. Throughout the semester, we worked under him and eventually submitted a paper. Prof. Batra’s fairness in acknowledging contributions is exemplary. Unlike other institutions where professors might publish papers without student recognition, he ensures that credit is given based on actual contributions.



Among many reasons, one of the big reasons I have great respect for Professor Batra is his unwavering dedication to his students’ growth. He puts forth tremendous effort to support and guide us in our careers. During my MS application process, Prof. Batra helped me define timelines for writing SOPs and CVs and preparing for tests, which was crucial for meeting deadlines and maintaining quality. His proactive approach in reviewing SOPs and CVs, along with assisting in university selection, demonstrated his genuine motivation for our success. He also connected us with relevant alumni to further aid our applications.



Whenever I have career-related doubts, Professor Batra is always the first person who comes to mind. This is the case even now, as I have graduated from college. After my internship at Skan.AI, I received a pre-placement offer while also considering pursuing a master’s degree abroad. Faced with the dilemma of accepting the PPO or requesting a letter of recommendation from my mentor, I turned to Professor Batra for advice. He recommended accepting the PPO, a decision that has proven to be excellent. I am extremely grateful for his guidance, which ultimately led me to my current role as a Data Scientist at Skan.AI.



In my eighth semester, I had the privilege of serving as a Teaching Assistant for the Machine Learning course. This experience was invaluable, as it allowed me to revisit the ML content, prepare industrial-level code, and experience the teaching field. What stood out most was Professor Batra’s immense trust in us, entrusting us with significant responsibilities that fostered a sense of importance and responsibility.
During meetings with Professor Batra regarding TA work, we occasionally forgot small concepts we had studied the previous year. In these instances, he never made us feel uncomfortable and patiently explained the details. Moreover, Prof. Batra’s understanding and consideration during personal issues further highlighted his supportive nature. As a TA, I had the rare and rewarding opportunity to teach a class of 250 students. This experience allowed me to explore the teaching field and realize how challenging it is to keep a large class engaged for 1.5 hours. It deepened my respect for Professor Batra’s exceptional teaching abilities.



Prof. Batra’s influence extends beyond academics. He instilled in us the importance of respecting time, maintaining discipline, and adhering to what is right rather than what feels good. He made us learn the importance of honesty.
In conclusion, my journey with Prof. Nipun Batra and the Sustainability Lab has been transformative. His guidance, support, and teaching have not only shaped my academic and professional career but also enriched my personal growth.

About me
I am Aabhas Senapati, currently a 1st-year undergraduate student at Harvey Mudd College, Claremont, California. I did my schooling in Ahmedabad, post which I took a gap year before coming to college. Aabhas Senapati working at the Sustainability Lab, IIT Gandhinagar

title: Curiosity Opens New Doors
text:
Curiosity opens new doors
This story starts back in 2019, when I was a grade 10 student at Zydus School for Excellence, Ahmedabad. It had been a couple of years since I had been self-exploring electronics and IoT-related projects and participating in online forums like Element 14 community and making various projects. One of my projects was ThingFinder, which I got incubated at GUSEC as a student-startup, without even fully understanding what a startup meant. This was probably one of the pivotal points, as it opened a plethora of opportunities in front of me, being part of the startup network in Gujarat, not just limited to grants and startup network, but also support from facilities like Nasscom at IIT Gandhinagar.
It was one of the events by IBM at Nasscom, IITGn, that someone suggested to me given my curiosity to learn and work on projects, I should reach out to Professors at IIT Gandhinagar and potentially work with them to learn and grow further. This led me to then look up Professors at IIT Gandhinagar who worked on Projects on similar lines to my interest and cold-mailed them with long paragraphs about who I am, what I like to do, and why I wanted to work with them. Reading back the old emails it seems such childish and poorly drafted emails and LinkedIn messages, yet three out of the nineteen Professors responded. Prof. Batra was one of only three Professors who responded to the mail and connected me with his Ph.D. student Rishiraj Adhikary, and then invited me to meet at IIT Gandhinagar. On my first meeting, Prof. Batra encouraged me so much and told me to continue my projects and also said that he would be happy to have me work with him during the summer. I am so grateful for this, had he not identified my potential and given me the opportunity early on my path could look very different.

title: Curiosity Opens New Doors
text:
Now comes uncertainty
I was very excited about this opportunity over the summer to be able to work at IIT Gandhinagar, especially given the fact that me and my peers were all preparing for JEE at Allen, from class 9, therefore getting to work at IIT before even attempting JEE, was something I was mildly proud about. But as they say, not everything is meant to work according to how you plan, and that’s exactly what happened, in 2020 came the coronavirus pandemic which disrupted my initial plans for the summer. It was not possible to be outside the home, and consequently, summer projects were also cancelled. Honestly at that point summer projects weren’t the priority either. But I still had a desire to work at IIT Gandhinagar, especially given that this was the only full-length summer break I would get before JEE I presumed. With the pandemic situation intensifying, I kind of forgot about working on a research project. But sometime during the summer unexpectedly, I got a message from Rishiraj bhaiya, that I would still be willing to work on a project remotely. While this was kind of unexpected given I had been dreaming to be at IIT Gandhinagar and work on a project in my fantasized view of a lab, I still was very excited to work on a project with them. This is how I ended up contributing my tiny bit of effort the Project Naqaab, where I designed a very simple led response to the ambient PM 2.5 levels, and retrofitted this setup onto a mask.
As I worked on this Project, my only expected outcome was experience, but to my surprise despite my almost insignificant contribution to the larger project, Prof. Batra, and PhD. Rishiraj included me as a co-author for the poster at UbiComp. Back then, I probably didn’t realize how generous it was of them to have me there and shows how people at Sustainability Lab value your contributions. In a world where people don’t give credit for significant contributions to academic research, as I look back to it, as a high-school intern, with minimal contributions got more credit for my work than I deserved.
This was my first experience working with the Sustainability Lab and Prof. Batra. After this, I also represented the project at the IRIS National Fair, but more or less this was like a good addition to my resume. Yet my desire to work at IIT in a proper research setting still remained unfulfilled.

This is after three years of first time interacting with Prof. Batra, as my friends were already planning to go to colleges, I was starting my gap year, with research working at Sustainability Lab IIT Gandhinagar. I was very excited as this was my first time staying by myself in a academic environment, and working on a full-fledged research environment. A typical day during that time was me waking up at around 7:30 am, finishing my chores and getting my breakfast, then going to lab around 9 am, and working on my targets for the week up till lunch, meeting new people at lunch and having sumptuous food, and then back at work up till dusk, then visiting other places around and playing foosball and air-hockey, having dinner, then playing volleyball, and back to conversations up till late night like 1 am and then going to sleep. While this might sound very simple, unlike my expectation of the academic environment to be a monotonous one, it was much more spontaneous and fun especially because of such supportive around like Prof. Batra and PhD. Rishiraj, who always kept the environment an engaging one beyond just the work. I was not supervised on a daily basis if I came at a set time or not, what time did I leave, but rather was given a sense of autonomy where someday I could take a day off, and someday I would work all night. I never felt as if I was burnt out, and always was checked in by both of them if I was enjoying what I was doing, if I was eating food properly or not and so on. Spending 5 weeks, everyone around campus became like a family, not just at Sustainability Lab, but even the housekeeping staff, or people from other labs at IITGn. A deep dive into the projects:
Naqaab: Given the ubiquity of masks during the pandemic and the high air pollution in large parts of the world, we used masks for health sensing and persuasion. We used masks to monitor health-related parameters such as temperature and lung activity. In our Project the smart mask, Naqaab, measured forced vital capacity (FVC) of the lung using a retrofitted microphone, aiding in early diagnosis of upper-lung disorders. I myself focussed on implementing the feature in Naqaab that measures pollution exposure and indicates via different LED colours for eco feedback based on local pollution levels. Naqaab Presentation
CO2 Monitor and SpiroMask: This Project was an extension of the Project Naqaabm where it focussed on using microphone to capture casual breathing patterns and calculate breathing rates along with forced breathing parameters. This project not only relied on audio based input to calculate the same, but also carbon dioxide sensors to get the data. This therefore also required as an additional component of measuring the Ambient carbon dioxide levels to offset the measurements, and also testing other hypotheses relating to carbon dioxide levels in public space. I specifically during my 5 weeks focused on developing this Ambient and portable Carbon Dioxide level data logger. SpiroMask Presentation CO2 data logger

The opportunity to work at an Institution like IIT Gandhinagar under the Guidance of Prof. Batra, offered numerous learnings both pertaining to research and just in general and wanted to share those below.

The first and foremost is definitely curiosity and pursuing moonshot ideas, was it not those I wouldn’t have got this opportunity in the first place. And more than approaching such amazing and supportive spaces like Sustainability, which are open to anyone who is enthusiastic to learn.
Secondly is a rigorous and determined approach, definitely something I had to work a lot on especially coming from a background of exploration and not academic rigour I lacked this ability. But working on the research and with the advice that I got from both Prof. Batra, and PhD. Rishiraj, both always emphasized on the importance of pursuing perfection in the work we did, and not just making things work by chance.
Then the next important lesson was documentation of one’s work, I heavily underrated its importance until I faced it the hard way, as working on projects, not only not having documentation hurts ones own progress, but also hampers other work. Most of the bottleneck in working on projects doing research I spent on figuring out how to navigate some errors which were not documented by other people. This underscores how important it is to document the work not just one’s milestones but also setbacks and errors, which is crucial for anyone to replicate the project in future.
In terms of a college/academic life, I also learnt the important role routine and discipline played, from eating food at right time, to doing your laundry, everything was important for a balanced and healthy time during the experience, and was a crucial skill that helps me till now.
While it may seem contrary to the previous one, having spontaneity and engaging with new people around be it lab-mates or people from other labs, fostered some of the best conversations and friendship during my time. Be it a a random table on lunch, or someone at maker-space, or walking through the hallway, its these interactions that stay with us forever. This spontaneity is what enabled developing a human connection with people beyond professional or academic environment, not just as a professor or guide, but as a mentor, friend and well-wisher for life, who are always going to support and root for you in your journey.

I am really grateful that I got such a transformative and life-changing opportunity to work with Sustainibility Lab, while it is definitely god’s grace and fate that I could get this experience, it is definitely to be highlighted that it wouldn’t be possible without supportive mentors like Prof. Batra and Rishiraj bhaiya, who gave space, opportunity and care to me in my journey. Definitely if you are reading this and considering to work at Sustainability lab, I can attest to the fact that the very least you would get is a bunch people who are there to support you in your journey in any way they can, it’s a space to not just grow academically or doing research but also a space to make friends and find lifelong mentors.

Sometimes, the detours are the best part of the journey!
It was the third year of my undergrad, I was looking for a Foreign Academic Summer Internship in Machine Learning or Computer Vision. I was having a hard time finding an internship. It was the same time I had enrolled myself in Prof. Batra’s Machine Learning (ML) Course. Believe me, he is the best when it comes to teaching. I was very disappointed about not getting a foreign research internship, and even though he didn’t know me, he was all willing to help me out. I had finally found a mentor in him. From the very same semester, I started working with the Lab and then onwards there was no looking back. And now whenever I think about my BTech, this lab was a big part of it. 
I have worked on 4 different projects and some open-source contributions for one and a half years. When the entire world was going crazy behind deep neural networks, it was under him that I explored the probabilistic machine learning models. And got a whole new perspective on ML. My first-ever project was on Deep Gaussian Processes for Air Quality Inference, though this was a course project, it never felt that way. There was continuous guidance from him and his PhD Zeel B Patel. Though we had limited time we were able to make significant contributions. We as undergrads (other collaborators Eshan Gujarathi, Saagar Parikh, and Sachin Yadav)  were able to publish our work as an extended abstract at ACM India, 6th Joint International Conference on Data Science and Management of Data CODS-COMAD 2023. title: Detours can sometimes be the best part of the journey!
text:
Deep Dive!
Building on my knowledge of Gaussian Processes (GPs), I delved deeper into the nitty-gritty of its working. In my third-year summer internship, I had the opportunity to work on Batched Gaussian Processes. It was this solo research that gave me a lot of confidence in myself and though it was difficult to understand the math behind GPs, Prof. Batra and other labmates were always there to help me out. Prof. Batra is extremely reachable, you just have to ask him and he will instantly set up a meeting and will explain everything with great passion every time. I just used to wonder at times, how passionate a person can be. The thing about this lab is that you don’t feel like you are working for the first time, so welcoming is the atmosphere. I still cherish the AB6 Workspace where we as a lab used to spend the entire day, have fun, and help each other. His feedback during research meetings might feel harsh at times but yes that always motivated me to work to the best of my potential. One of the best parts of working with this Lab is that Prof. Batra knows what our future goals are and accordingly assigns projects to students considering his/her interests. I still remember that he knew I was applying for a master’s and he put me on an application-based project and pushed me to publish a paper in AAAI or NeurIPS. Until then I had never even dreamt of such a publication. 
And guess what I was successful in publishing my work on Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM) using Bayesian deep learning strategies like Gaussian Processes in the NeurIPS workshop on Gaussian Processes in 2023 (collaborator: Gautam Vashishtha). A lot of credit goes to Prof. Batra and PhD Zeel. It was my experience of GPs from the summer that helped me quickly get going with this tough problem. And this work of mine has to be the highlight of my BTech. This work not only molded me into a good researcher but also taught me numerous life lessons. Prof. Batra’s dedication in academia as well as in day-to-day life always motivated me to do better each day. Every time I used to go with some updates on the work done, he would always point out even the minutest details, you might feel does it even matter. But believe me, it does, this makes you perfect at what you do, not only in research! I learned how to write good papers, and how to do productive research. “Drawing conclusions or insights is the key to any research problem” - were always the words of Prof. Nipun Batra!
This project had lots of ups and downs but he always pushed me whenever I felt low and felt like the project was not heading anywhere. But you have to trust Prof. Batra and follow his advice especially when you feel everything is going down the spiral. Prof. Batra’s words still echo in my ears, never run behind publications, and don’t think much about the end goal. Just focus on your current work, set smaller milestones, and keep producing results and you will never know when you will have a flurry of publications. Isn’t this relevant to anything you do in life, just focus on the present! My last work with this lab was on Multi Output models for air quality inference. Every new project feels like a new challenge but when you have an excellent mentor and support in the lab the job is half done. By the beginning of this project, I started enjoying research. To touch on another aspect, I had never realized the importance of open-source contributions unless I joined this Lab. The excellent environment at the lab of always helping ML society, helped me make contributions to Dr. Kevin Murphy’s (Google Researcher) Book.

title: What It Means to Be a Part of the Sustainability Lab
text:
Who am I?
Hi, I am Kalash Kankaria, a 2024 graduate of IIT Gandhinagar and a proud member of the Sustainability Lab. I graduated with a B.Tech in Computer Science and Engineering, spent close to two years working as a Data Scientist at Skan AI in Bangalore, and am currently pursuing an MS in Computational Finance at Carnegie Mellon University.
But before all of that, there was IIT Gandhinagar, Machine Learning, Prof. Nipun Batra, and eventually, the Sustainability Lab. This is a little about what that journey meant to me.



The Sustainability Lab batch of 2024 at graduation, May 2024.




Outside the Lab
It feels strange to think that I took my first Machine Learning course around the time ChatGPT had just been released, and Prof. Nipun was already asking us to experiment with it as part of an assignment.
It is not an exaggeration when I say that ML (ES654) was probably the only class where I never felt like sleeping. The lectures rarely felt like textbook study. Concepts were presented in a way that made you visualize what was happening, question why it worked, and understand where it could actually matter.
That course was also the first time I worked on a project under Prof. Nipun. One of his requirements was that every project report be written and formatted almost like a prospective research publication. At the time, I remember wondering whether all that effort was really necessary for a course project. Looking back at those reports now, I understand exactly why he insisted on it. We were being taught much more than just how to finish an assignment.
Fast forward to the next semester, when I formally joined the Sustainability Lab for a project course while simultaneously taking his Probabilistic Machine Learning class. Our research was, in some ways, connected to ideas from the course, but it never felt repetitive. If anything, the classroom gave us the tools, while the lab showed us what happened when those tools met an open-ended problem with no answer waiting at the back of a textbook.
In my final semester, I got the opportunity to TA the very Machine Learning course that had drawn me into the field in the first place. That experience made the circle feel complete. With Prof. Nipun, being a TA was never limited to grading assignments. We were encouraged to conduct tutorials, take vivas, explain concepts, and engage with students. It strengthened my own understanding enormously and gave me a small taste of what teaching actually feels like.


The Lab
It is relatively easy to guide a student who already understands how research works. Teaching someone how to think about research—how to approach an open-ended problem, figure out which questions are worth asking, deal with uncertainty, and slowly turn an idea into a meaningful contribution—is much harder.
That is probably the most valuable thing I learned during my year at the Sustainability Lab.
My primary work was around Bayesian Unlearning, but the biggest learning went far beyond the specific problem I happened to be working on. I learned how to take an unfamiliar research question, understand why it matters, study what has already been attempted, question existing approaches, identify what might be missing, and then work towards making our own contribution.
Prof. Nipun managed a balance that I now realize is extremely difficult to get right. We were never spoon-fed solutions, but we were also never left without direction. There was enough freedom to explore, get things wrong, and develop our own ideas, while still having the guidance needed to move forward when we were stuck.
The lab itself has an energy that is difficult to capture in words. It is full of exceptionally talented people, but what stood out to me even more was how approachable everyone was. Discussions happened naturally, people helped each other, ideas moved across projects, and there was a genuine excitement about figuring things out. It never felt like everyone was simply working on their own isolated research problem.
What distinguishes the Sustainability Lab most for me, however, is the intention behind the research.
The projects are not built around technology simply because a particular technology happens to be exciting at the moment. They begin with real problems. The underlying question is often: Can the advances we are making in computing, machine learning, and AI be used not just to make things faster or smarter, but to make something meaningfully better?
That philosophy personally resonates with me a lot. There is something incredibly motivating about working on technically challenging problems while knowing that the eventual goal extends beyond the technology itself.
Perhaps the simplest way I can describe my experience at the Sustainability Lab is this: after almost every meeting with Prof. Nipun, I would leave the room wanting to immediately get back to work on the ideas we had just discussed.
For me, that says more about the research culture of the lab than almost anything else could.


Even After That
One might assume that once we graduated, the connection with the lab would slowly fade away. For me, that was never the case.
As a farewell gift, Prof. Nipun gave each of us a book with personalized impressions and messages about us. It was such a small but deeply thoughtful gesture.
About a year and a half into working in industry, I decided that I wanted to pursue a master’s in quantitative finance. Even though this was a very different direction from the research I had done in the lab, Prof. Nipun was one of my biggest supporters throughout the process. From writing a recommendation letter that got me into CMU, to later connecting us with people in the relevant industry whenever he came across an opportunity, that support did not stop just because I was no longer his student.
And every time I visited IIT Gandhinagar after graduating and met him again, it somehow never felt as if so much time had passed. The conversations were still just as easy, the lab still felt just as welcoming, and there was always the same warmth that I remembered from my time there.
I think that is what ultimately makes the Sustainability Lab more than just a place where I did research for a year. The projects end, courses finish, and people graduate, but the mentorship and relationships somehow continue beyond all of that.
And I believe they always will.

title: 10 Things I Would Say to My Day-One Self Before Joining Sustainability Lab
text:
Hey there! I’m Aditya Mehta and I joined the Sustainability Lab in my 4th year. Yes, pretty late, and I still regret it. I walked in thinking I was just going to do a project in a lab. I walked out feeling like I’d been part of a group of people who really cared about what they were building. If I could go back and talk to day-one me for five minutes, this is what I’d tell him.
Some context first. From August to November 2025, Jiya Desai and I worked on a weather forecast emulator and a web app built around it, mentored by Deena Lad and advised by Nipun Sir. Global forecasts like GFS are coarse (about 27 km grid cells), while the regional WRF model gives finer detail (9 km) but is expensive to run. So we trained a vision transformer to take the GFS forecast and predict the WRF-style 2-metre temperature field, and it reached an R² of 0.98 on our test set. Alongside it we built a web app on Hugging Face where you can pull in atmospheric data, plot it interactively and run Microsoft’s Aurora air pollution model without touching a raw NetCDF file.



Presenting our project poster at the UG Research Showcase.


So here are 10 things I would say to my day-one self.

1. This is not going to be like any other lab.
Forget how project courses usually go, where nothing happens for twelve weeks and then everyone panics in the last three. It doesn’t work like that here. There’s a weekly catch-up, so every week you need to have something to show, even if it’s small. That sounds like pressure, but being around people who are all working hard makes you want to keep up, and research just becomes part of your week.


2. The data is going to be messy. Very messy.
You’ll walk in thinking about models and architectures, and then spend a big chunk of your time finding, collecting and cleaning data. The lab works on real sustainability and environmental problems, so the data never shows up in the neat format you were hoping for. Different sources, missing values, formats that don’t match. Some days feel like data archaeology. It’s annoying, but a model is only as good as its data, and real problems come with real data.


3. Learn to tell the story behind your work.
Presenting isn’t just putting your graphs on a slide and explaining the axes. You have to explain what you did, why, what went wrong and what you think the results mean. The weekly meetings are good practice, so take them seriously and get comfortable talking about your blockers. Knowing something and explaining it well are two different skills, and the second one will be useful long after you’ve left IIT.


4. “It didn’t work as expected” is a perfectly good answer.
There will be weeks when you’re wondering what on earth you’re going to show Nipun Sir. The idea didn’t work, or the model did badly, or you ended up exactly where you started. Your first instinct will be to make the result sound better than it is. Don’t. In our own project we tried several different ViT training setups (scaling the parameters, masking NaN channels, adding static variables, fusing in a projection vector), and only one of them ended up being the best configuration. Just say what happened. He’ll ask why and help you work out the next question. It’s quite freeing to work somewhere a failed experiment is treated as information and not as a failure.


5. Document everything. Future you will be grateful.
Please document your work every week. You’ll think you’ll remember why you made that dataset, or which version of the code made that graph, or why you changed that one parameter. You won’t. Three weeks later you’ll be staring at final.ipynb, final_new.ipynb, final_v2.ipynb and final_latest.ipynb with no idea what happened. A clean repo, proper versioning and some notes feel like boring housekeeping, but they save you hours, and someone else might have to pick up your work someday.


6. Use AI. You are in the right place to experiment with it.
Treat AI tools as force multipliers, not crutches. Use Claude and ChatGPT to write code faster, debug stubborn errors, and digest complex papers, but never stop thinking critically. You still need to understand what you’re asking and spot when the output is wrong. Developing that judgment early is what will make you a truly effective researcher (and it’s the exact habit that prepared me for my upcoming role as a Gen-AI Developer at Barclays Investment Bank)


7. Find your “why”.
This matters more than you think. There will be weeks where all you do is clean data and debug, and results won’t be enough to keep you going. What helped me was remembering what the lab is actually about: using AI for a more sustainable future. When you see your work as a small piece of that, you stop just pushing a metric up and start trying to understand a real problem.


8. Be grateful for the people you’re doing this with.
I was really lucky to have Jiya Desai as my project partner. Research is hard enough on your own, and it helps to have someone with you for the good experiments, the bad ones and the “why is this not working?” moments. We also had Deena Lad as our mentor, who guided us through the ups and downs of the project. Somewhere between all the meetings, datasets and presentations, they stopped being just a teammate and a mentor and became friends. You’ll make bonds here that go beyond the work.



A lab meeting at the Sustainability Lab, where we were all twinning.




9. Make a personal connection with your mentor, not just a professional one.
Some of my best memories with Nipun Sir have nothing to do with research. Take the time to talk to him about other things and get to know him as a person, not just as a professor. I still remember him giving me The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People with a personal note written inside. It was a small gesture, but it has stayed with me more than a lot of the technical discussions we had.



The copy of The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People that Nipun Sir gave me, with his note.




10. One day, you are going to miss this.
This is the one I most wish I could get through to day-one me. You’re always focused on the next experiment, the next meeting, the next presentation, and before you know it, it’s over. Along the way there are moments that make you realise how much it meant. For us, one of those was the UG Research Showcase, where we ended up as runners-up for Best Project Presentation. Technically runners-up, but let’s not get too technical about a good photograph. Look at that picture and think about everything before it: the messy data, the weekly meetings, the failed experiments and the small wins nobody else saw. That’s what it all turns into. And of course the Akshardham Trip, which I am not going to spoil for you now, but is going to be one of the core memories of your life.



With the Director of the institute at the UG Research Showcase, as runners-up for Best Project Presentation.


So that’s it. Don’t just try to finish your project, let yourself become part of the lab. Ask questions, get your hands dirty with the data, show the bad results, find people you enjoy working with and talk to your mentors. Every once in a while, stop thinking about the next deadline and look around. I joined in my 4th year and I still regret not joining sooner. But one thing I’m sure about: I am really, really glad I joined.

title: Efficient Time Series SSL via Signal Descriptors
text:
The problem and the idea
Unlabelled sensor signals already contain structure: their distribution, their variation over time and their frequency content. This work uses statistical, temporal and spectral descriptors as targets for self-supervised pretraining.
A feature extractor computes descriptors from each signal window. An encoder and a prediction head learn to predict these descriptors directly from the raw signal. The resulting representation can then be used for downstream tasks. This pretraining objective does not require signal augmentations or contrastive pairs.



Conceptual method diagram: the raw signal supplies descriptor targets and inputs for an encoder trained to predict them. This is an illustration, not experimental data.

title: Efficient Time Series SSL via Signal Descriptors
text:
What was evaluated
The final manuscript describes 1,440 experimental configurations across two wearable sensing benchmarks, four backbones, two label fractions (5% and 100%), and frozen and unfrozen fine-tuning settings.

HHAR: activity recognition from inertial sensor data.
PPG-Dalia: heart-rate estimation from wearable signals.

Methods are compared using aggregate ranks over configurations. Feature-based supervision is among the strongest approaches on these tasks at lower estimated training compute, measured using network passes. This is not a measurement of total deployment latency or energy use.

title: Efficient Time Series SSL via Signal Descriptors
text:
Performance and training compute
The two panels below are reproduced from Figure 2 of the camera-ready paper. Lower-left positions are preferable: better average rank with less estimated training compute. TSFEL labels denote the descriptor-based methods.





Heart-rate estimation on PPG-Dalia: descriptor methods occupy the low-compute region, with TSFEL90 obtaining the best average rank shown.







Activity recognition on HHAR: TSFEL90 obtains a similar average rank to Barlow at lower estimated compute.

title: Efficient Time Series SSL via Signal Descriptors
text:
Build on it
The practical takeaway for wearable-sensing researchers is a simple pretraining baseline that is worth testing when labels and compute are limited. The open code supports reproducing and extending the comparison.

“an effective yet underexplored source of self-supervision”
— Paper abstract, describing time-series descriptors

title: Efficient Time Series SSL via Signal Descriptors
text:
Scope
The evaluation covers two wearable datasets and short fixed-length windows. Descriptor choice remains an inductive bias. The results do not establish universal superiority across time-series tasks or show that every learned representation is interpretable.
An earlier version, “Feature-Informed Self-Supervised Learning for Time Series Understanding,” was presented at the MiLeTS workshop at KDD 2026.
